subsubtopic: EXTENDED USE OF SOCIAL INSURANCE NUMBERS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
In view of the expressed intention of Canadian General Electric to use the social insurance number as part of an identification badge system in its Peterborough plant, and considering the opposition of union officials and workers who regard this use of the social insurance number as unfounded and a threat to their personal privacy, I ask leave to move, seconded by 419-582-028, commonly known as the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That this government and the present Minister of Employment and Immigration cease their apathetic and indifferent attitude toward the expansion of the social insurance number in the public and private sectors, and introduce immediately legislation giving individuals the right to refuse the use of their social insurance number to any organization which does not have specific authority provided by federal statute, and making it obligatory for any organization which wants to make the social insurance number an employee identification number to have the informed consent of the individual.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to deal with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that the Minister of Employment and Immigration stated in the labour committee on Thursday night last that the young people of Canada were prepared to be spoonfed and would, if given a chance, "sit at home, suck their thumbs and wait for the unemployment insurance just to pour in", since this has been proven not to be the case by studies done by the Department of Employment and Immigration which show that young people want to work, and by other studies which show that young people actually under-use the unemployment insurance program in relation to their actual percentage of unemployment, and since the National Union of Students has demanded an apology for this gratuitous insult to all of Canada's young people, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Rae):
That this House call upon the Minister of Employment and Immigration to apologize for his intemperate statements.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN FOOD PRICES-ACTION TO CURB PROFITEERING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Yesterday, a spokesman for the Department of Agriculture predicted that food prices in the coming year would increase another 10 per cent, such increase taking place after the products left the farm gate, that is to say, at the retailing and processing level.
Has the minister had an opportunity to investigate the report of the Economic Council of Canada which I brought to his attention over a week ago? It shows that profits in the food industry have increased some 63 per cent in the past year. What will the minister do to ensure that this level of profiteering will not continue into 1979?

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN FOOD PRICES-ACTION TO CURB PROFITEERING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have looked into the report referred to by the hon. member, the report put out by CSIP. To begin with, I must say that parts of that report were misunderstood and were not read in conjunction with other parts. On the other hand, I think the report was misleading in certain parts and also is subject to criticism in some parts. I should point out that the CSIP report dealt with both food and liquor, including beer, wine and hard liquors, whereas the AIB report dealt with only food.
The CSIP report dealt with only 20 firms in its survey. It had no information about those firms, whether they were large or small, whether they had been on strike, or whatever. On the other hand, the AIB report dealt with 81 processing firms and 14 retailing firms making up two-thirds of the food business. The CSIP report compared the first quarter of 1977 with the third quarter of 1978. That is a very unusual procedure because of seasonal differences in the food business. The AIB report compared the first half of 1977 with the first half of 1978.
Finally, the unit of measurement used in the CSIP report was profits per unit of output, which is not used on a regular
December 12, 1978

basis as a comparative measure. The AIB report used gross profits before taxes as a percentage of revenue. On the whole, I and many others feel the CSIP report did not give an accurate assessment of profits in the food industry. We are still concerned about increases in food prices next year. A report I have indicates that increases of approximately 14 per cent this year will decline to approximately 9 per cent next year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. It relates to a disturbing report made last night, which I am sure the minister would want to clarify, concerning possibly charging refugees coming from Vietnam the cost of their transportation by Canadian aircraft to this country.
Since this may mean a cost in excess of $1,000 for each refugee, most of whom have come here with little or none of the wherewithal to cover this basic cost, could the minister clarify this unusual situation and, hopefully, incorrect report?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF CHARGING VIETNAMESE REFUGEES FOR AIR PASSAGE TO CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the report is correct. It is normal policy to require payment to be made. In the past, most immigrants once established have willingly paid this amount. If they are not able to do so, the Crown invariably wipes out the loan. But many immigrants like to repay the loan. There is a revolving fund available to help people in this particular category, and those who have been helped often want to repay. That is the basis upon which the transportation cost is collected: it is normal policy.

been clarified with the United Nations High Commission on Refugees?

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF CHARGING VIETNAMESE REFUGEES FOR AIR PASSAGE TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in connection with another proposed refugee movement from Argentina, I think the minister is well aware of a recent communication from myself, the hon. member for Montmorency and the hon. member for Greenwood, concerning the situation of 100 political prisoners. The authorities in Argentina agreed to release these people if they could be guaranteed sanctuary in a country. After direct representations by the three of us to the officials in Argentina some time ago, it was indicated that Argentina would be quite happy to release these people.
Since there seems to be some difficulty in having any of these people released, even though some interviews have taken place, I wonder if the minister could indicate what steps are being taken with the Argentinian authorities in order that they may act in good faith with respect to the very serious plight, with prolonged detention and in some instances torture, of the people presently being held in Argentina.

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF CHARGING VIETNAMESE REFUGEES FOR AIR PASSAGE TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, representations have been received and we have made representations to the Argentine authorities concerning 68 people who are being detained. In some instances the officials will not concede that these people are in prison, and in other cases they have indicated that where another country has expressed an interest in an individual, they will not give us access to that particular person in jail.
We have now interviewed two people. One person has already been admitted to Canada in a quiet way so as to protect his anonymity. Argentina has now indicated that we will be permitted to interview, I believe another 12 people, but has yet to concede that the total number of names we have submitted are in fact of individuals in prison there. However, we are pressing on with a very difficult situation.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF PUBLIC SERVICE RETIREMENT BILL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the President of the Treasury Board with respect to the government's proposals dealing with Bill C-12, the public service retirement bill which is before the House with respect to which a specific invitation was addressed to members by the government House leader. This bill, according to the government House leader, will not be reached by the end of the year or by the time we recess. speakeroldname: Hon. Judd Buchanan (President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF PUBLIC SERVICE RETIREMENT BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have an opportunity to indicate my plans to the House. As the President of Privy Council
Oral Questions
indicated at the end of last week, in view of the large number of groups which have indicated they would like to comment on this bill and make their representations before the committee we came to the conclusion that it would not be possible to have the bill in place before the end of the calendar year. Therefore, it is our intention to proceed with it early next year.
The provisions relating to indexation, in which I think the hon. member is particularly interested, would not come into effect on January 1, 1979. In fact, we would have a one-year hoist and the three-year tranche would run for the calendar years 1980, 1981 and 1982. We do not anticipate there being a retroactivity clause in the bill.

Also, I think a couple of technical provisions other than the ones relating to air traffic controllers would become operative.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of questions for the Minister of Labour who is responsible for the new centre for occupational health and safety.
Many persons who worked with asbestos during the Second World War in a Defence Research Board plant at Ottawa have been afflicted with serious asbestos-related diseases. I believe four people have died in recent years. In view of this situation, I would like to ask the minister if he is considering setting up procedures to identify all the employees of wartime defence plants who may be similarly at risk from asbestos exposure, to determine if they have developed asbestos-related diseases and to compensate them and their families for the suffering involved.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MONITORING OF AND COMPENSATION FOR WORKERS EXPOSED TO ASBESTOS HAZARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that question arose in the "late show" last night and we gave a preliminary answer to the hon. member. I have asked my department to try to determine what we can do, as the Department of Labour, to assist these people in this matter. The responsibilities may be shared among several departments, but we do have it under consideration. I hope to give a more complete answer at a later date.

subsubtopic: MONITORING OF AND COMPENSATION FOR WORKERS EXPOSED TO ASBESTOS HAZARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question. It has been documented in court cases now under way in the United States that Canadian asbestos companies were aware as early as 1949 of the potentially fatal health hazards to which their employees were exposed, but they still took no action to inform their workers.

I would like to ask the minister if he would consider setting up a government fund for victims of asbestos-related diseases, in order to assist them to bring civil actions against companies and corporations which knowingly failed to alert workers to the danger of working with asbestos.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: MONITORING OF AND COMPENSATION FOR WORKERS EXPOSED TO ASBESTOS HAZARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will certainly consider that representation. And so that no one will be under any misunderstanding, I should point out that most of the health and safety in enterprises in Canada fall within provincial jurisdiction.
I do not want to give an answer this afternoon that will leave the impression that the federal government intends to intrude into provincial jurisdictions. However, where there is a federal establishment where persons may have worked with asbestos in the past, we will accept our responsibility. In fact, we have the equivalent of a workmen's compensation fund at the level of the federal government: it is known as the Government Employees Compensation fund. Moneys are set aside to compensate injured workers or those whose health has been damaged, so long as they fall within the limits of federal jurisdiction.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
that Bill C-9, respecting public

December 12, 1978
Referenda
referendums in Canada on questions relating to the Constitution of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to move second reading of Bill C-9, the referendums bill. This bill is being introduces by the government at a critical time in Canada's history. I am sure all hon. members recognize its potential importance. The bill provides the framework which would permit parliament to approve that referenda be held on questions relating to the Constitution of Canada, where that includes all the conventions and enactments of the constitution as well as the political and judicial processes of Canada.
I want to deal with three themes in my remarks today: first, the need for the bill; second, its implications for parliamentary democracy and for federal-provincial relations; and third, the principles underlying it as the framework for a democratic procedure.
[ Translation]
Canada has clearly entered the decisive stage of the constitutional debate which has been active since the early 1960s, but which goes back to the 1920s-if not beyond-and the first attempts to deal with the problem of an amending formula. The debate is exciting and it is necessary. Canada today is radically different from the four colonies which drafted the British North America Act 111 years ago. Where then there were four provinces and three million Canadians, during the past 111 last years, Canada has been transformed from a rural frontier society into a strong and sophisticated industrial state.
Where then-that is in 1867-we came almost exclusively from British, French and native ancestry, now we include an important fourth stream-that 30 per cent of Canadians who come from continental Europe, from Asia, and the other continents. While in 1867, it took months to travel from the Gulf of the St. Lawrence to Vancouver Island, now we can do it in hours, and our messages and images can do it instantly.
Where then the state played a relatively marginal role in most people's lives, today it has grown to absorb 40 per cent of our gross national income and to touch our lives in ways never then dreamed of.
Given these enormous changes, we must have the greatest respect for the Fathers of Confederation who drafted our constitution. It has served us well and provided the framework for extraordinary accomplishments. But it is necessary that Canadians look carefully at this constitutional legislation to ask whether, after over a century, the time has not come to renew our most basic law.
And this, of course, is exactly what is happening. The government has worked actively to promote this review: first, with the white paper "A Time for Action" last June; secondly, with Bill C-60 setting out possible changes; and, most recently,

in late October, with its recent offer to discuss a number of questions relating to the division of powers.
The recent constitutional conference was a success, I do not hesitate to say so. It is now being followed by intensive discussions by the federal and provincial governments on a number of significant items. The justice ministers and the ministers of federal-provincial affairs or intergovernmental affairs have already held a three-day meeting.
Another one is scheduled for tomorrow night or rather for Thursday morning. It will be held in Toronto and will last for three days, ending after next Saturday's meeting. This conference will allow us to further examine the constitutional proposals which have been discussed during the recent first ministers' conference in late October and early November. But whatever the prospects for agreement on these constitutional issues may be, I for one am confident that real progress will be made during the conferences and discussions which will take place in the coming weeks.
So whatever the prospects for some agreement on some questions, it is clear that the Canadian public is not yet directly involved in the process of constitutional change. I believe there may be circumstances when such direct involvement could be of the utmost importance. For instance: It could serve to acquaint the large majority of our citizens with the importance and character of proposals for constitutional changes and permit the people to express themselves directly on these proposals. Even if the proposals were supported by the great majority of federal and provincial governments and by the important political parties, such public participation on the process of constitutional change could be very valuable.
This involvement of the public in the constitutional reform could directly demonstrate the legitimacy of the constitution and help transform this legal document-which is out of necessity somewhat dry-into a people's statement of their basic principles which would guide them over many decades. Direct public involvement could also serve to guide the federal and provincial governments, should the process of constitutional revision ever become blocked. Obviously, a referendum in these circumstances would not be entered into lightly. As well, any federal government would be aware of the great risks of defeat in a referendum if it asked parliament to approve a question with important provincial governments or parties ranged against it.
The referendum bill before us, Mr. Speaker, would do nothing to minimize those risks for the federal government. As a matter of fact, under this act, the federal party would not get more than 20 per cent of the television time allowed by the CRTC to the various political parties. And provincial parties generally would get as much television time as federal parties. These and other measures ensure that no federal government would ever be in a position to manipulate the result of a federal referendum over the opposition of the provincial governments or opposition parties. But the federal government
December 12, 1978

would be able to ask parliament to approve a referendum question if it was confident that a public vote on the question would clarify the desires of the population in regard to constitutional reform.
These are two circumstances, and 1 could quote others, when a federal referendum may prove very useful in constitutional reform. There is another reason for this bill, Mr. Speaker, and it relates to the particular challenge to the country posed by the present government of Quebec. The Parti Quebecois, as is known, is committed to holding a referendum on the constitutional future of that province. I do not know what the question will be and nobody at present seems to know, not even the government itself which is eventually supposed to ask the question. 1 honestly hope that both the question and the Parti Quebecois' option will be clear so that the Quebec referendum will serve to clarify the desires of Quebeckers. But whatever the precise question and option, I think it is beyond question that the Quebec government is committed to an end to a federal Canada, that is an end to Canada based on two orders of government, each directly elected and having real powers to tax and to spend within its competence. Given these goals of the Quebec government and given that it has equipped itself to hold a referendum on the future of Quebec, the Government of Canada believes it is incumbent on itself and on parliament to ensure that we are equally equipped to consult with the people of Quebec, or of the other provinces, or all Canadian citizens at the some time, if need be.
Canada is a federation, and a federation requires a careful balance between the central and provincial governments. Canada and its provinces have parliamentary systems of government with well established principles and traditions for the political process. Some Canadians, and I respect their views, are worried that a law which would enable parliament to approve referendum questions on constitutional matters may have serious implications for either our federal system or our parliamentary democracy. Are they right to be worried?
Let us first consider the question of our federal system. It is basic to the present bill that referenda be consultative only. They would not be binding on parliament. This means that a federal referendum would not serve to replace the present procedures for constitutional amendment. This is clear in the bill, it is quite clearly spelled out, and it was clear in the bill which was introduced in the last parliament. This position is maintained in the present bill. It is therefore not a substitute for parliament, not a substitute for our present rules of constitutional amendment, but it is an addition to the present procedures, an addition which might provide extra relevance or legitimacy or which might help to move the federal and provincial governments closer to agreement.
What is more, as I indicated in the Elouse in April, the government believes it is clear that if a question which had
Referenda
implications for one or more provinces was posed, then consultations would be held with those provinces relative to that question. Finally, the procedures set down in the bill for the referendum campaign are designed to put the federal and provincial governments and federal and provincial political parties on a completely equal footing in such a debate. Thus, the rules of a referendum campaign would preserve the balance in our federal system.
Let me go to the second question or the second area of concern which some Canadians feel, and that is the concern for our parliamentary democratic system. Here I think three points are critical. First of all, referenda would be consultative in nature. Second, they would only be held on the authority of parliament; and third, they would be restricted to subject matters having to do with constitutional questions.
First, the consultative nature of referenda would ensure that parliament was still responsible in every way, as it is at the present time, for the actual approval of any constitutional amendments. Because referenda would be consultative, it would also be possible to distinguish between the form of referendum questions and that of constitutional amendments. There may be occasions when it would be appropriate to ask the public to pronounce on broad constitutional principles or on the general characteristics of political structures without becoming involved in all the details which characterize the legal description of these. Thus parliament and the provincial legislatures would continue to be concerned with the detailed examination of legal texts, but they might do so after a public expression on the larger question; and it would always be possible for parliament or a legislature to reject the views expressed in the referendum were its members ready to answer for this in a general election when their turn comes. That is how the democratic system functions.
I hear some hon. members on the other side laughing. Let me remind them-although perhaps this is not a good example to quote to them-that Mr. Levesque has said quite clearly that he would not consider himself bound by the answer he would receive in the next referendum and certainly would not intend to resign; but quite clearly in such a case he would be called upon to account for his decision before the electorate at the next provincial election, which would also be the case for any other government, provincial or federal, in a similar situation.
Therefore, I repeat that nothing would be changed in terms of our present system of proceeding with constitutional amendments. Referenda would provide parliament and the legislatures with the benefit of the views of the Canadian people expressed in a specific way on a specific subject at a specific time.
Second, only parliament itself can approve referendum questions. This is the most basic protection of the parliamentary system because members of the House would never permit our system to be eroded by the reckless use of referenda. It is worth noting that those countries which make extensive use of referenda, especially Switzerland and some American states, have procedures for citizens to initiate referenda by petition,
2036

December 12, 1978
Referenda
and it is these petitions which are largely responsible for the frequent use of referenda. These referenda take place at the initiative of a certain number of citizens, as provided for either by the state constitution, in the case of the American states, or by the national constitution, in the case of Switzerland. However, in country after country where there is no right of initiative by petition arising out of a group of citizens, the use of referenda has been extremely limited.
Finally referenda would be restricted to constitutional questions. This type of restriction is found in many countries with parliamentary systems. There is no evidence that the possibility of constitutional referenda is the thin edge of the wedge which leads ineluctably to referenda on other questions. Even the Mother of Parliaments, the parliament of Great Britain in Westminster, has held two referenda in recent years; one in Northern Ireland and another one throughout the country concerning the entry of Great Britain into the European Common Market.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Both divisive.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Those referenda were held on constitutional questions. Moreover, the Mother of Parliaments recently approved two more referenda on the constitutional future of Wales and Scotland.
Also, 1 might draw the attention of the House to the fact that Australia, Denmark, France, Ireland, New Zealand and Norway are all parliamentary democracies which hold occasional referenda but which restrict their subject matter solely or almost entirely to constitutional questions. I have not included in this list other democratic countries which use the technique of referenda on various subjects over and above constitutional questions. The most obvious ones which come to mind readily are the United States and Switzerland.
Of course, there is a logic to restricting referenda to constitutional questions. The constitution is the basic law of a country. It establishes the structure of the state and the sovereign relations between parliament, people and the different orders of government. In some countries, sovereignty is deemed to flow directy from the people. In those cases it is entirely natural, through constitutional referenda, that people should determine the institutional form which sovereignty should take.
In Canada we consider parliament is sovereign within its domain. But even here, most would recognize that people are the most important source of sovereignty. Consultative referenda permit the population to express itself on questions of sovereignty without violating the legal sovereignty of parliament or of the legislatures.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to describe the principles on which the government has based the proposed procedures for referendum campaigns and voting. But in doing so, I want to avoid entering into details, for the nature of this bill is

necessarily complex and, obviously, it would be better to get into them at the committee stage of debate. The government has based the bill on certain broad principles, which it hopes make the bill a model for referenda in a federal state. Besides, we have had consultations with opposition parties when the legislation was first presented during last session. However, the government recognizes that a bill of this type-like the electoral law-should as much as possible represent the views of all parties on proper procedures for a political contest. I want to underline, therefore, that we approach the debate on this bill with an open mind, Mr. Speaker, and we hope to work in as close co-operation as possible with all parties to ensure the procedures are widely acceptable as the best possible. In this regard, I think our debate at this stage is especially important because it gives us the opportunity to examine the principles underlying the bill before entering into details.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that members opposite will recognize that in some cases no procedure could be devised which fully satisfied all our principles. We had to make difficult choices between principles to which we all believe in this House. I am confident the opposition will recognize these difficulties and that in its criticisms it will show full regard for such difficulties. So these are the major principles underlying this bill. First, the procedures governing a referendum should be fully consistent with all those political rights normally respected in Canada, especially freedom of expression and freedom of association. Secondly, the procedure should impose financial controls which encourage a fair and open debate.
I want to discuss these two principles together, Mr. Speaker, because they are so closely related in the provisions of the bill. If we had been concerned only to ensure freedom of association and freedom of expression without any financial controls our task would have been greatly simplified. In fact, it is the combination of this freedom of association and of expression with the need to exercise some financial controls on the other hand which is so challenging. Our analysis led us to conclude that it would be impossible to satisfy both principles by trying to impose over-all financial controls on the "yes" and "no" campaigns within a referendum campaign.
The Quebec government, in its referendum legislation, has decided to impose such over-all financial controls on the two opposing sides in a referendum. An in-depth study of this bill has convinced us that the approach and the policy adopted by the Quebec government necessarily leads to infringements of the freedoms of expression and association.
December 12, 1978

Hon. members of this House will certainly want to voice their opinion on this matter-this is a very serious issue-and they will indicate how, by legislatively forcing people to join umbrella organizations representing each side of the question, the freedoms of expression and association of these same people are necessarily reduced and restricted. One can even suppose that, since only two unbrella groups are recognized, some people could be excluded from the referendum debate because they would be rejected, for political reasons by one or the other option or umbrella group. That has indeed happened in other countries. We have seen this in Norway, in particular, during the referendum debate concerning the country's entry into the common market. There have indeed been cases where two major organizations were created-they were not established by law-for and against the proposal, and for purely political reasons, certain groups could not join either one of these organizations, which believed that politically it would not serve their purpose to have some small group, considered marginal for example, join them lest it would discredit the opinion of the majority. We have therefore concluded that this requirement set out in the Quebec legislation to have all citizens join either one of the two umbrella organizations is a serious infringement on the freedom of association and even on the freedom of expression. That is why we have rejected that alternative, but only after due consideration, we have studied it with a great deal of interest and attention. We have examined foreign experiences in this respect and we must note that that philosophy, though it may be inspired by apparently defensible motivations prompting toward control over expenditures made by the two opposing groups, results in an undue and unecessary limitation of the freedom of association and the freedom of expression which must be the two basic freedoms in any self-respecting democratic system.
So what did we do? Barring, an over-all financial control over the two groups in question we found another solution. And the solution we found is that which is contained in the bill which we think is an acceptable way of dealing with the problem of financial control by limiting the expenditures and contributions of individuals and legal persons, as opposed to the "yes" and "no" campaigns; in other words, what we are going to control is the contribution from each individual or legal person. Thus, there will be a maximum contribution so that no one will be able in the referendum debate to exert undue pressure as a result of his wealth as his contribution will be subject to a maximum set out in the legislation, but we are not preventing anyone from contributing and particularly not from joining one of the tens of hundreds of groups that can form in a debate like that.
In short, this procedure avoids the situation where citizens are simply forced to join either one of the two camps and being practically prevented from particm-ting freely in the referendum debate outside those two camps. Modern democratic
Referenda
views require that the public be informed of the provenance and object of political funds and that there be limits on the use of these funds. The Canada Elections Act limits the amount which individual parties and candidates can spend, but does not limit the size of contributions. And that is rather easy because there is a limited number of political parties. There are now four parties in the House and at election time there are always a few more, some that do not even manage to have one member elected to this House, but one must admit that the number of political parties is relatively limited. But if we are talking about a referendum debate for example on constitutional matters, obviously the question will have to be answered by a yes or no, but each political party, each group, each association, might want to decide pro or against such or such thesis, for entirely different reasons; some groups, I repeat, might prefer not to be associated with others in such a political debate or democratic debate.
Because we were not prepared to force the creation of "yes" and "no" groups which would be subject to total expenditure limits, we chose to put a limit of $5,000 on the amount that an individual or legal person can spend or contribute. No person, no corporation, no union could make a contribution exceeding $5,000 during the referendum campaign. That sum seems sufficient to permit anyone a natural extension of one's freedom of expression while it also ensures that no one or no group can have an unfair advantage because of private wealth or because of a special position which they might have, as corporations, unions, non-profit associations of any kind which would have access to special funds.
Mr. Speaker, the procedures in this bill recognize federal and provincial parties as basic actors in our political process, but they facilitate the creation of groups or even unbrella groups, should parties or individuals want this. But they do not make it compulsory, this must be emphasized. They also permit individuals to act alone, should they so wish, with absolutely no need to register or report on their activities. Thus, they preserve freedom of expression, subject only to the limit of $5,000 which applies to contributions or expenditures.

Mr. Speaker, I have taken some time to elaborate on the first two principles that guide us in this bill, and that is that first and above all we should respect freedom of expression and freedom of association in the referendum debate; and, second, there should be some financial control on the powers that may be exercised by those who are contributing financially.
There are two other principles I should like to talk about which we find in this bill. The third principle is that the procedures should ensure the probity of the referendum process at the same high level as the probity of the electoral process. The fourth principle is that procedures should be as simple and as familiar as possible. Thus, the bill before us uses the procedures of the Canada Elections Act wherever possible. When adaptation has been necessary because it is impossible

just to prescribe the Canada Elections Act, we have tried to make it as consistent as possible with electoral practice.
One example is the introduction of representatives of provincial parties or of referendum committees into the revision of electoral lists and scrutiny of the vote. Another example is in basing the allocation of television time to parties on the procedures established for elections.
This practice for the allocation of television time involves a difficult choice because there is a counter principle whereby time would be allocated equally to the yes and no groups. We decided against this partly because we could not devise a satisfactory procedure for the equal allocation of broadcasting time without forcing the creation of umbrella groups and violating the freedom of association and the freedom of expression about which I spoke earlier.
More fundamentally, we believe that broadcasting time should be allocated to recognized spokesmen for the population in relation to their established support in reference to provincial and federal political parties. If those parties wish to reallocate their time to outside groups, to divide it with other supporters, they would be free to do so, but the total allowable broadcasting time would be divided between federal and provincial political parties. Adopting the procedure from elections and from the elections act seems to do this perfectly.
The final and fifth underlying principle is that the procedures should respect the federal nature of Canada and not favour parties or groups active at the federal level over those active at the provincial level. I have already touched on this principle in discussing the implications of referenda for our federal system. Again, the government's bill is a marked contrast in this regard with the referenda act approved earlier this year by the Quebec National Assembly. While the federal bill gives full rights to provincial parties to participate in a federal referendum, the Quebec bill gives absolutely no rights whatever to federal parties to participate in a Quebec referendum. At best members of the federal parties, and I mean here members of this House, will only be able to participate as a privilege, if they are accepted by the referenda committees, the umbrella committees, set up by members of the National Assembly.
In any event, this bill would ensure that any referendum question was given a full and fair debate by all federal and provincial parties and any other interested groups. It ensures that there will be no bias in favour of the so-called "Ottawa point of view" against that found in provincial capitals.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, to conclude let me say that this bill seems to me necessary and important, that it is a positive addition to our federal system and is fully consistent with our parliamentary system. It is based on democratic principles which are largely endorsed both in this House and beyond, particularly by provincial legislatures. Therefore, I invite opposition members to approach this bill in a positive spirit of critical examination, so that together we may try to improve its provisions and prepare Canada for the decisive phase of its constitutional development. I would like to thank hon. members from this side of the House as well as the other side who in recent months have expressed their views and thoughts on that very important issue. Once again, as I said early in my speech, not only has the federal parliament a right to get an instrument as proposed in this legislation, but in the present circumstances I think the government would be irresponsible if it failed to propose to parliament a legislation such as the one before the House today and which, I am sure, will be discussed positively by all parties.

speechtext: Would the minister tell the House whether in this bill-and I have read Bill C-9 through very carefully- there is any provision which provides, after the referendum has been completed, for any option to be taken? Or is it that the opinion secured by the referendum is purely advisory, and it would still be left to parliament and legislatures to exercise the same jurisdictions they now have?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the interpretation in the latter part of the hon. member's question is the proper one. The referenda under this bill will be purely consultative, and there is no action required by parliament or by any legislature following any particular result of any referendum.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Or by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION

Or by the government; obviously by the government. If there is, for instance, an overwhelmingly positive answer to a positive question in a particular referendum and the government does not proceed to do anything about it, surely the people of Canada would ask themselves why they had to go through that exercise in the first place. That would be the responsibility of the government of the day, vis-a-vis the citizens of Canada after having expressed their views.
I reiterate that it is clearly a consultative process. There is nothing in the Constitution of Canada at the present time that could make the result of a referendum binding on the government, parliament or any particular legislature. I can assure the hon. member that the rights of parliament, the legislatures and particularly our responsibilities as parliamentarians vis-a-vis the amendment of the Canadian constitution continue to lie completely and wholly within the legislatures and the federal parliament.

speechtext: Jointly and severally.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Perhaps at some point we will have that matter clarified.
This is one of the most important, one of the most major, bills ever to come before the Canadian parliament, because by its very nature it has tremendous bearing on our established political process. This bill gives to the governor in council, the cabinet, the executive, power to initiate referenda on constitutional matters. Nothing could be more substantive or more serious. It is serious not just because of its constitutional aspects, with which I shall deal in a few minutes, but it is doubly serious because a referendum of any kind at the national level is a serious matter in itself.
We have not had much experience with national referenda in this country, one reason being that the whole concept is alien to the spirit of the Canadian parliamentary system; but the experience that we have had has shown that, far from being a mechanism of unity for Canada, the referendum has had the opposite effect. I say that sorrowfully, Mr. Speaker. The referendum of 1898 on prohibition and the referendum of 1942 on conscription were divisive and left their mark on this country.
In both cases the province of Quebec voted one way and the rest of the country voted the other. No one who knows even a fragment of Canadian history can be unaware of the incredibly divisive effects of the conscription referendum of 1942. The wound has not healed to this day and is, in fact, one of the major historical events which underlies much of the current disunity. Whatever reasons one can cite for favouring referenda, the healing of wounds is not one of them. Referenda serve to set neighbour against neighbour, family member against family member, and the cleavage remains long after the content of the referendum has been forgotten. We must bear this fact in mind if we are looking to national unity as a factor in this bill.
The last thing we want at this time is to further rend the fragile fabric of confederation at a time when it is being subjected to greater strain than ever before in our history. Being aware of its potential for divisiveness we must, if we are
Referenda
to consider referenda as an integral part of the political system, arrive at that decision only after careful thought, only after thorough examination of its effects on our parliamentary system; and, above all, we must arrive at it with the utmost honesty.
I do not find this legislation before us today to be in that spirit of honesty and forthrightness which this difficult subject demands. I see this legislation as being devious, dangerous and even deceptive. It purports to be an act respecting public referendums in Canada on questions relating to the Constitution of Canada. It is, instead, a blatant attempt to subvert and undermine the responsibilities and duties of the Canadian system of responsible government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: You must be kidding!

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: If this bill were merely dangerous, our course would be clear. We would simply vote against this nonsense and have nothing more to do with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: But devious?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
It is devious, as the minister has said, and deceptive as well. The government has undertaken to dress up this bill in attractive and worthy clothing of direct democracy, constitutional change and even national unity. We must not let this disguise deceive us for it conceals a fraud, the chief result of which would be to bring about not simply constitutional change-because we are all interested in that-but a constitutional revolution by stealth.
Of course, it would be done in the name of simply giving the Government of Canada powers equal to those which the Parti Quebecois government has given itself. That is not fighting fire with fire, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would have it and as the Minister of Justice would have it. That is trying to fight fire with gasoline, with the result of burning down your own house and of spreading the fire much further-to fires of disunity.
I want to discuss the real significance of this bill because it demonstrates once again that this government either does not know what it is doing, where it is heading, or it does not want the rest of the country to find out. The bill has many defects and there are a number of ways in which we might deal with these.
Some time ago the separatist government of the province of Quebec began preparations for a referendum on the future of the status of that province in Canada's confederation. All of us watched with considerable concern as the arrangements were announced, piece by piece, by which the separatists would try to take our country apart, piece by piece. We watched that process with concern and alarm. We know that the people of Quebec will be called upon to express their wishes on this country's future. On this side of the House we are confident, even if the government is not, that the people of Quebec will

December 12, 1978
Referenda
reject any attempt to trick their country away from them by a misleading plebiscite or any other illegitimate means.
Our greatest concern is not that the people of Quebec will fail to see through the propaganda of the separatists, but that the government opposite will continue in its blind, wilful and divisive ways to the point where it discredits the federal system in the eyes of all Canadians.
Sir, the government says that it needs this legislation, that it must have as much power to consult the people of Quebec as have the Pequistes. On the surface that appears to be a very reasonable argument. If that were what this bill meant and all that it meant, we on this side could accept it fairly willingly. We would have no problem with that kind of legislation if that is what it were. All of us are concerned that the Quebec referendum be conducted in a fair way. But already it is quite clear that the Pequistes are loading the dice as well as stacking the decks.
The existence at the federal level of a clear set of rules to assure the utmost freedom of speech and the utmost in full debate prior to holding any referendum in the province of Quebec is very important. If nothing else, it will constitute a clear warning to the Pequiste government that it must play more fairly than it intends at that time.
Establishing these rules well in advance of the actual asking of such a question by either Quebec or the federal government is also important, for then parliament can concentrate its attention on the precise questions to be asked and the circumstances in which they will be asked without being distracted by debate over procedures. That is also good. We do not argue those points because, as I say, they are good.
However, what is not good, what is devious and deceptive, is the scope of this legislation. What is not acceptable is the attempt once more to sneak into the hands of this most untrustworthy government, and to seek to do it unilaterally, even more power to manipulate and abuse this parliament and the people of Canada than it already has.
Hon. members will recall that last Tuesday, on the initiative of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), this House engaged in a debate which demonstrated the extent to which the government has gone in undermining the Canadian parliamentary system of responsible government. That debate showed how this government had rejected and refused to put into play those rules and practices which would enable us in the House to have real parliamentary democracy. This government persistently rejects the basic constitutional principles of holding itself responsible to and properly accountable to members of the House of Commons.
If this bill should pass in its present form, it would give the present government even more opportunity and more incentives through abuse of the referendum process to evade proper accountability in this House. Today, under the pretence of meeting the Pequistes' power with equal power, the government opposite proposes a constitutional revolution. That is what this bill is all about.
We on this side are always willing to discuss and advocate, long before the government was prepared to do anything about it, discussion on constitutional evolution. However, revolution of this scope? Where on earth is this government leading us?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Perdition.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
The terms of this bill are far too wide. Let me read that part of clause 2, the interpretation section, where the scope of this bill is effectively defined. It sets out what the government would see as falling within its power at the national level. In dealing with referendums on the constitution, it defines the constitution, that area where the government could conduct referenda. It states that the Constitution of Canada includes, and I quote:
-without limiting the meaning of that expression,
(a)	the customs, conventions and enactments that comprise the Constitution of
Canada, and
(b)	the political and judicial institutions and processes of Canada;
If the bill had stopped after (a), despite my reservations on the "without limiting" phrase, that might have been acceptable. However, the inclusion of (b) opens up the question almost to the four winds. Canada has a great many political institutions, political processes, judicial institutions and judicial processes. A great many of those political institutions, political processes, judicial institutions and judicial processes are not now, ought not now or ought ever to be, under the authority and jurisdiction of the central government. They are under the jurisdiction of the provinces and rightly so.
That is what our constitution asked for. That is why we have a federal system. That is why we have a federal constitution, despite this government's constant attempts to subvert and centralize all power in Ottawa as far as it can. This is another indication of that tendency toward centralization which this government has exhibited year after year. We can see that tendency coming to the fore.
Clause 3, dealing with proclamation of a referendum, reads as follows:
Where it appears to the governor in council that any question relating to the Constitution of Canada or relating to or arising out of a proposed or possible change in the Constitution of Canada is of sufficient importance to warrant obtaining the opinion of electors on that question, the governor in council may, by proclamation, direct that the opinion of electors be obtained on that question by putting the question to the electors of Canada or of one or more provinces specified in the proclamation at a referendum called for that purpose.
That is a referendum called on any constitutional question by the Government of Canada. That wording in clause 3 encompasses any constitutional question that the Government of Canada might want to ask. That is how wide the scope of this bill is.
In his remarks the minister said that questions put on a referendum are restricted to matters of a contitu.ional nature. What kind of a restriction is that, given the scope of constitutional matters in our federal system?
A myriad of concerns come to the fore, concerns which all of us as parliamentarians, representatives of the people, feel deeply about. Who is going to determine whether or not an

December 12, 1978

issue is constitutional? Can the federal government call a referendum on constitutional issues that might or would have a bearing on provincial or concurrent jurisdictions without the approval of the provinces? What about a referendum on controversial constitutional matters that have not yet been assigned to either provincial or federal jurisdictions, such as offshore resources?
If it wishes, a majority government could use its majority power to see that referendum results would be carried into law. The minister said this would only be a consultative mechanism. However, in the explanation that accompanied the Canada referendum bill, the section on page 5 dealing with the legal character states: "Referenda would be advisory or consultative in nature. Such referenda may, of course, be morally binding if the government indicates its intention to be so bound."
What would happen if a majority government decided to use its majority power to push a referendum through? In the case of offshore resources, for example, could the government effect a decision of this issue by means of a referendum, using the results as a directive to the government and thus do an end run around the courts? Is that the kind of thing the government has in mind with this legislation?
A general provision for referenda on constitutional matters is in itself a constitutional change of some magnitude. Some it is a constitutional innovation. Since it is something new that is coming before us, a matter of great magnitude with regard to constitutional change, should it not be included as part of an over-all package of constitutional reform? Is that not where this bill belongs? Is that not where this suggestion or innovation belongs?
If that kind of general power is what the government wants, then let it deal with it in the proper place and at the proper time. In the meantime, however, there is nothing to prevent the government holding a plebiscite on a particular subject as it did with conscription, or as the United Kingdom did in the case of the common market or on Northern Ireland. Contrary to the impression the minister tried to leave before the House, those matters were dealt with as specific bills coming before the parliament at Westminster in order to deal with a specific question at a specific time. That has been done before in this House, and it can be done at any time.
My greatest concern is that the present government is moving away from past experience where a referendum or plebiscite was held on a specific matter arising at a given point in time. They are moving away from that practice. They are now arrogating unto themselves a general power to hold referenda on constitutional matters. They are now using the Quebec situation to create a new and formidable weapon for the Government of Canada.
Now, sir, it could be argued that it would be appropriate for us to introduce the general concept of referenda into our political system. That is a legitimate argument. There might be arguments in favour of such a course but there are no
Referenda
arguments for doing it this way, trying to slip it in through an underhand method, nor can there be. The method being used by way of this bill is an extension of the government's penchant for attempting to change our federal system unilaterally, something which we have seen so much evidence of in recent months. It is before us once again.
I wish to draw attention to what has gone on in recent months. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that last spring the House and the country were given a white paper on constitutional change. It was called "A Time for Change". That white paper was designed to encourage public discussion and input into the whole process of constitutional change. But no sooner was the ink dry on that white paper than we were handed a finalized formula in the form of Bill C-60, the constitutional amendment bill. Before the people could even receive copies of the white paper we were presented with that bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women

speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
All the minister has to do is look at the dates on which those two documents were presented and he will find that this was the method which was used. Of course, the government was quick to tell us that the legislation itself was open to discussion, that none of it was immune to change. However, in its usual way of saying one thing and doing another, the government's subsequent actions put the lie to those dubious assurances. I say this because the Prime Minister in his most recent utterances has made it clear that his intent remains to meet his deadline for constitutional change regardless of opposition, regardless of the opposition of the provinces, regardless of the damage to the federal system.
A parliamentary committee, after much study, recommended the wholesale redrafting of Bill C-60, the government's proposals for constitutional change, but with the admonitions of that committee still ringing in his ears the Prime Minister met the provincial premiers to discuss the whole spectrum of constitutional questions at the first ministers' conference in the latter part of October.
The outcome of that conference, one which the Minister of Justice attended, was the establishment of a top level federal-provincial committee under the chairmanship, I believe, of the Minister of Justice to work in such areas as amending formulae, the division of powers, institutions, the whole field of constitutional change. That is why the committee was set up- to deal with matters such as the very one we are debating today. While that committee was working in this area thinking it would really have some influence on constitutional change, the government House leader introduced a major piece of legislation, one with great constitutional ramifications, which gives it and it alone the power to hold referenda on any question related to the constitution including, if the remarks of the Prime Minister are any indication, questions with which that federal-provincial committee is dealing at the present time.
I just want to quote, at this point, from the proceedings at a press conference given by the Prime Minister on October 21 of this year. He was asked what specific question or questions he

December 12, 1978
Referenda
would like to put to the Canadian people in a referendum. In response, the Prime Minister had this to say:
I indicated that the questions could have to do with as simple a thing as patriation of the constitution, or repatriation of the constitution; they could have to do with the will of the country to remain united, and they could have to do with anything in between.
"Anything in between"-anything of a constitutional nature. If there really is a reason for changing our system to accommodate referenda-and that may well be an arguable case-why is this concept not part of the federal-provincial discussions presently under way? How often is the government going to break faith in matters of federal-provincial relations? What is the minister going to say to his counterparts when he meets them on Thursday to explain why he is doing something unilaterally in the House of Commons which he will not discuss with them?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: I would say you are talking nonsense.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Try to be more intelligent than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
How much longer does the government intend to continue its history of unilateral action on major constitutional matters without input from the provinces? What hon. gentlemen opposite must recognize is that the constitution does not belong to one particular government at one particular time. Nor do our institutions or the judicial processes. The government must give up the idea that it holds all the power and that it can impose its will upon Canadians for all time. I say this to the minister very seriously: it is not the prerogative of a dying government to extend its constitutional will long into the future.
We have heard a lot of talk recently from ministers and from the Prime Minister himself about direct democracy. Does the government really believe in direct democracy? I have the impression that it does not. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) have spoken about ways in which direct democracy might be practised and the idea has been put forward by any number of people in the Liberal Party. They have persisted in talking about consulting the people on every important or emotional issue that comes up. They talk about it, but when this legislation comes before us we find they have not dealt with the essence of what they were seeking to convey to the public.
This bill is not about direct democracy in the manner in which the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport have spoken about it. This bill uses that broad concept, but it is applied only to constitutional matters. Either we should be speaking about specific legislation tied to a specific object, the Quebec referendum question, or we should be talking about the introduction of direct democracy on a grand scale.
Either one of those is a legitimate issue to be discussing, but we on this side would be willing to discuss the specific legislation to which I have just referred which would address itself to the Quebec referendum question. If that is what the government judges to be necessary, we want to make it perfectly
clear that we would be willing to discuss that kind of legislation. What we object to is the potential to have any and all fundamental changes to our constitution brought about in this fashion, and that is what this bill would do.
As it stands, this bill would constitute very significant constitutional change. We on this side have always said that in the debate about constitutional change other participants from all levels must be brought into the discussion. I am talking about the other partners in confederation as well as the people of Canada. They must be brought into the discussion of any proposals for constitutional change, of which this bill is a very major one.
Evidently the government does not plan to do that. It does not plan to consult any of the other legitimate expressions of Canadian thought and feeling on this major constitutional change.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: It has been out for six months.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
This legislation may or may not be wholly within the power of parliament to pass. I am not sure of that, especially when I consider the way in which provincial powers would likely be trampled on if this government were given the wide ranging power it is asking for through this bill. With this bill in the hands of an unscrupulous government, that government is given greater potential for seizing power than it is given by the Emergency Powers Act or any other piece of legislation presently on the statute books. That is what this bill does.
Of course, the government-and I know the way it approaches these things-will probably say this bill is within its legal power, and well it might be because that is the course the government took with its previous constitutional bill. Bill C-60. We know the objections to that approach which were raised by constitutional experts, by the provinces and by people all across the country. We know that that line of unilateral action which this government has always put forward has been rejected time and again.
The government should try to decide what it wants to do with this bill. If it wants fundamental constitutional change of the kind envisaged in this bill, it must bring the whole debate out into the open and into a much wider sphere of discussion. It must consult the premiers, the provinces, the public and other constitutional specialists outside government. If, however, the government is serious in its intent about wanting only to deal adequately with the Quebec referendum question, then this bill should be amended to do that job-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: You have not been doing your homework.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
-and to do it without giving the government even more wide ranging and arbitrary powers than it already has. What the government should not be doing in any case is trying to do the first of these jobs under the guise of the second. That is what we have in this bill.
The government is trying to use the Quebec situation to delegate to itself much greater constitutional powers. What we

December 12, 1978

need in this case is a special committee on constitutional matters. We need that committee to be set up in this House and to look at this bill. The committee should be given this bill so that it can get the terms and the mechanics of referendum legislation and referendum questions settled to everyone's satisfaction as quickly as possible. Then the committee could get down to the business of establishing once and for all the proper scope of questions which might be asked of the people of Canada.
That is the nub of this bill: What is the scope of questions which one level of government can put to the people of Canada? What is the power that the federal government is seeking to usurp? Before a committee of this kind we could look at this question and hear witnesses who are able to advise not just the government but all members of parliament on constitutional matters. Then we could see precisely what devious objectives the government has in mind and deal appropriately with them.
Either we live in a federal system and respect the basic tenets of that federal system, or we do not. Either we work out our constitutional renewal jointly with the provinces, or we repudiate our system of government. Either we encourage both levels of government to work together to build this great country of ours, or we engage in an ever greater proliferation of legislation directed against all provincial governments-not just one-which could prove divisive and destructive not just to our political system but to our whole country. The broad scope and powers embodied in this bill could do just that.
In a situation like this, and in the escalating confrontation with the provinces which this government seems determined to bring about, who speaks for Canada?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: We do.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as both the minister and the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) have already said, this bill is important, and it certainly is related to a fundamentally important part of the history of our country. There is no doubt in my mind-nor I am sure in the mind of any member of parliament-that we would not now be debating a measure to provide the Government of Canada with the right to have a referendum on constitutional matters if we were not already faced with the hypothetical possibility that one province, namely, Quebec, will take steps which could lead to the breaking up of our country and to the independence of that province.
In addressing ourselves to the question of a referendum we must consider not simply the general principles involved in parliamentary democracy and the general question of referenda, which are important in constitutional matters and in other matters, but it is very important that we consider, as always in
Referenda
politics, the historic context in which a particular proposal is being dealt with, whether at the federal level or any other level.
I say with all respect to the person who has just spoken that I have rarely heard a more contradictory speech in all my life-

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: -in terms of facing the political reality in Canada. It is certainly my view in general that in a parliamentary democracy, or in any other kind of democracy, the referenda idea is not a good one, as a general principle, to deal with all kinds of matters. I hope hon. members opposite will listen to the debate because I will support the bill in just a minute and give reasons for doing so.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
As a general proposition, men and women throughout history, whether you consider Greece at the time of Pericles, or England at the time of John Stuart Mill, or Canada and the rest of the modern world today, most responsible democrats, in my view, have argued that it is the role of elected people to make decisions, that it is our responsibility to face immensely complicated issues and to work out answers and compromises, because that is essential in a democracy, and normally referenda do not provide for compromise. Normally they divide a community on an issue, and frequently they are inappropriately used because they are used on matters which should be questions of personal morality. So in the view of my party, referenda on a whole range of questions are not something that a democracy should be concerned with. Democracy should be concerned with electing men and women to study issues seriously, to recognize the complexity of most problems and to work out a fair solution.
Now I want to come to the bill before us and to put it in its historical context. I wonder where the Conservative party is in its thinking, and I say that seriously. We will have a serious debate on this issue. The province of Quebec has elected a government honestly and democratically made up, from their perspective, of decent, honest and good citizens. I will not denigrate them because 1 happen to differ profoundly with them about the future of our country and indeed about the future of their province. But the historical reality is that, for the first time in the history of our country, we are confronted with a government which was elected in part, so they interpret it, on a mandate to divide the country. So it is not the present Government of Canada but they who were the first historically to present us with a bill that will provide in one province the right to decide.
I say frankly that if we recognize-be it in Canada, in Ireland, in Pakistan or in other parts of the world-two distinctly different cultural and linguistic entities like those we have in Canada, which have existed so far with some real tensions-and most of us hope we can work them out and

continue with a united Canada-or if a society is divided on religious grounds, as it is in other parts of the world, we will have to resolve the issues at some point by having a vote.
