subsubtopic: REDUCTION IN WAITING PERIOD FOR MARRIAGE DISSOLUTION
speechtext:
that Bill C-207, to amend the Divorce Act (living separate and apart), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, once again I am pleased to have an opportunity of bringing the topic of divorce before the House. This time my bill is Bill C-207, an act to amend the Divorce Act (living separate and apart). The explanatory notes read as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to reduce to 18 months the three to five-year waiting period required for a marriage that has broken down to be dissolved. It also eliminates the question of fault under this ground for divorce.
It was 11 years ago this month that members of the House of Commons were debating Bill C-187, an act respecting divorce. At that time the government felt it was time to reform Canada's archaic divorce laws and to bring them into line with the social climate of the 1960s.
Prior to 1968, the only effective ground for divorce in every province-save Nova Scotia-was adultery. Most provinces entered confederation without divorce laws or procedures, and it was not until after 1930 that they were granted the authority to establish provincial divorce courts. However, residents of Quebec and Newfoundland were required to apply for a parliamentary divorce because these two provinces had no divorce courts until 1968. In 1966, the question of divorce reform was referred to a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons. Its report on divorce was presented to parliament in June, 1967, and in 1968 the Divorce Act became law.
The act retained many of the traditional marital offences as grounds for divorce, but it also included a modified concept of marriage breakdown as a new ground for divorce. One of the grounds established was a separation period of three to five years-three years separation if the petitioner is the non-deserting spouse, five years separation if he or she is the deserting spouse. This separation ground conferred on each married person significant powers of individual control as to whether he or she desired to remain married. Today, about 40 per cent of all divorces are based on this ground.
It is important to remember, Mr. Speaker, that although the government was anxious to modernize our divorce laws, it was conscious of Canadians' interest in maintaining the sanctity of marriage and of the family unit. It is in this same light that I have put forward an amendment which will reduce to 18 months the three to five-year waiting period required for a marriage which has broken down to be dissolved. It also eliminated the question of fault under this ground for divorce.
Also, Mr. Speaker, some members may feel that my bill is tantamount to tinkering with the present divorce law because it is not consistent with the remaining marriage breakdown sections in section 4 of the Divorce Act. I would be prepared to put forward an amendment which reduces the waiting period in all circumstances to 18 months.
Let me take a moment to outline the divorce legislation of other countries with regard to the concept of marriage breakdown and the period of separation. Several countries differentiate between unopposed and opposed actions. For example, In England the waiting period is two years if the divorce is unopposed, and five years if it is opposed. Norway requires a one year separation if the action is unopposed, and two years if it is opposed. In Australia, the family law act of 1975 states that a ground for divorce is established if the parties separated and lived separately and apart for a continuous period of not less than 12 months immediately preceding the date of filing for the dissolution of marriage. The separation need not be agreed upon by both parties.
Sweden, in 1973, introduced divorce on demand, which includes both unilateral and consensual dissolution of marriage. Either spouse is at any time entitled to have the marriage terminated on formal request, without having to show separation for a period of time, marital offence or irretrievable marriage breakdown. The state's function is to approve the request. The only qualification provided for in Swedish law is a "reconsideration" period of six months if the divorce is opposed or if the family contains children under the age of 16.
In the United States, some states, namely, California, Michigan, Georgia and Nebraska, have adopted divorce by consent. Divorce by consent subjects marriage to the joint will of the parties involved and limits the involvement of the court or state. In fact, in Canada it is argued that because 90 per cent of our divorce cases are uncontested, divorce by consent already prevails. Hence, it is often recommended that the government may as well legalize its present existence.
Since the enactment of the 1968 Divorce Act there have been a myriad of studies, reports and recommendations, all concerned with the divorce issue. The concepts of divorce on demand, divorce by consent, marriage breakdown and others are constantly being debated and reworked by various legal groups, people involved with the status of women and by religious affiliations. One of the foremost bodies engaged in
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
December 12, 1978

this examination of our divorce laws is the Law Reform Commission of Canada. The commission has published proposals in the form of studies, working papers and reports in an attempt to formulate a cohesive legal policy for the Canadian family.
The commission did examine the subject clause of my proposed bill and has advanced several arguments against the imposition of a designated period of separation as a prerequisite to divorce. It referred to the dilemma faced by an economically dependent spouse who may be forced to leave the matrimonial home, and also to the hardship faced by responsible spouses who encounter marriage breakdown yet must go through the loneliness of an enforced period of separation, being neither married or unmarried, in a coupled society.
Professor Herman R. Hahlo, who presented a research paper entitled "Reform of the Divorce Act, 1968 (Canada)" to the Law Reform Commission, also examined the three-year separation period and recommended that it be reduced to one year. He reasoned thus:
To take a large slice out a person's life by withholding a divorce long after the prospects of reconciliation have vanished can only be explained by a conscious or subconscious desire to punish a spouse for seeking a divorce. Many experienced marriage counsellors suggest that six months are normally sufficient to determine whether there is any hope of reconciliation-
Professor Hahlo also touched upon the five-year period imposed on the deserting spouse and recommend that in this case, too, the required period of separation be reduced to one year.
It was in May of 1976 that the Law Reform Commission promulgated its recommendations. Why has divorce legislation remained unchanged to date? That is my question.
Lirst of all, it was deemed important that divorce reform not proceed until such time as all the provinces had enacted matrimonial property laws which would effect an equitable division of property on dissolution of marriage and in a manner which would protect the spouses who are not financially self-sufficient. However, at this point in time, eight of the ten provinces either already have passed such a law or are in the process of drafting legislation. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I feel that this rationale is no longer credible and that we should proceed now to provide the desired reforms.
Secondly, it has been proposed that some measure of jurisdiction over divorce may go to the provinces as part of constitutional reform, thus making it unnecessary to have the federal government introduce divorce reform. I am of the opinion that constitutional reform should not delay the implementation of new divorce legislation, and in fact it may be a long time before some consensus is reached on this point. The number of studies, reports, etc., which have been brought forth in recent years attest to the fact that now is the time for divorce reform.
A letter forwarded to me from a concerned citizen points this out, very well. This letter was actually received by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) and it contained a request that a copy be forwarded to me. I should like to read one paragraph of the letter which refers to my previous bill on
Marriage Breakdown
this same topic, formerly Bill C-214 which was debated on second reading in December, 1977. The paragraph of the letter to which I refer reads as follows:
The object of this letter is to add at least one voice to the demand for revision along the lines recommended by the commission. Perhaps you would pass along a copy of this letter to Mr. Robinson and hope that he or some other member would see fit to reintroduce legislation to benefit those persons in our society who are hopelessly trapped in the present restrictive law when society generally would be in favour of giving them freedom.
When people are considering amendments to our current divorce laws, one fundamental question is considered paramount: How will this affect the institution of marriage and the family unit? Divorce statistics since 1968 do lend credibility to those opposed to divorce reform who argue that making divorce easier will hasten that decline of the family unit. However, I am sure that all hon. members agree that family strength is a matter of moral values combined with a personal commitment. Legislation cannot create marital bliss or preserve family unity, nor can divorce legislation lead to the breakdown of the family. As it was pointed out by the commission, "it is not divorce that destroys families but bad marriages."
I think everyone should bear in mind, however, that official divorce statistics merely tell us about the number of divorces. They tell us nothing about marital conflict and disruption. Not every marriage breakdown ends in divorce; a couple may choose to continue to live together in disharmony rather than participate in a divorce process which is often painful.
Therefore, the correlation between divorce rates and the collapse of the institution of marriage is indeed difficult to prove. How is the reduction of the length of required separation going to affect the stability of marriage? The Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons on Divorce in its report made note that, in establishing the period of separation, the prime consideration should be whether the period provides a fair test that the marriage in question has in fact broken down. As I see it, the time required must be sufficiently long enough to give the couple a chance to reconcile their differences, but not so long as to force individuals to remain in unsatisfactory and unhealthy relationships.
It is extremely important, especially where children are involved-for an unhappy marriage is a detriment to children-that the parties be able to dissolve their marriage as painlessly as possible in order that they may build a new life and provide a more healthy, positive environment for themselves as well as their children. To quote Professor Wolfgang Friedman:
People should be able to live out their lives as joyfully as possible under conditions which enable them to develop their personal capacities and potentialities. This means the right to correct errors, the right to cast off a burden that has become intolerable and may lead to the sapping of vital energies and the moral fibre of the affected parties.
Throughout my speech, Mr. Speaker, I have quoted statistics, briefs of the Law Reform Commission and professors to enhance my argument. However, I believe the most profound

December 12, 1978
Marriage Breakdown
testimony comes from a private citizen, and I would like to read his letter into the record:
I am writing to express my support for Bill C-207, an act to amend the Divorce Act (living separate and apart).
It appears to me that there can be no basis either in policy or in philosophy for any member of parliament to vote against this bill, as it does not change or add to present grounds of divorce, and has no effect on property, maintenance or custody provisions. In allowing a so-called deserting spouse to sue for divorce after 18 months, it recognizes what is most often an irreconcilable marital breakdown, and erases what is presently a two-year "sentence", that is the forcing of a deserting spouse to wait five years rather than three years (which is presently Canadian law). The present waiting period has resulted in a statutory conviction of the deserting spouse for his guilt in having made his decision to create a new life for himself. As anyone who has been married will most readily verify, guilt is almost never one-sided.
The proposed amendment does not, in any way, obliviate the requirement of the court to ask about the possibility of reconciliation, nor does it affect any awards of maintenance or custody, or division of property. It seems in keeping with the present thrust of the federal government in the area of human rights. It is of no value to society or to the family unit to force an unwanted and often harmful relationship to continue legally. The present law allows couples three years to build up deeper resentments, to threaten each other with litigation and to use emotional blackmail, often in the form of one spouse's refusal to give the other his or her freedom for reasons usually based in spite, malice, anger and resentment. Children are the unfortunate, innocent bystanders, and for three to five years are torn between their parents' court dates, lawyers and threats. No party can stabilize his or her position until the final decree absolute, and many lives may be held in hurtful, expensive and unnecessary suspense for years. As everyone realizes, the result of such situations is, all too often, contrived grounds and manipulations to get into court. Surely the very fact of such manipulations is sufficient to point out that the law is not in keeping with the needs of the Canadian public.
I can in no way believe that the fabric of society or of the family will be damaged or diminished by this amendment. A family held together in name only is not a healthy unit... a clean and quick break is most often the solution for the immediate problem and the most beneficial act for a quick recovery.
I most sincerely urge the support of this bill and hope that members do not so lose themselves in self-righteousness that they overcome their ability to sympathize with people who need the law and the legislators on their side.
I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that my bill is the magic solution. However, it does attempt to bring our divorce laws in line with current thinking and perhaps helps to pave the way for additional divorce reform and strengthening of the institution of marriage. 1 hope all members will support may amendment and refer my bill to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for further consideration.

speechtext:
1 would like to congratulate the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) for presenting a private member's bill on a matter which, I know, is of great interest to the public of Canada generally. The ground in the act which my good friend would like to amend is chapter D-8, section 4(l)(e) of the federal statutes dealing with divorce which became law in 1967 and 1968 by chapter 24. The section reads:
(e) the spouses have been living separate and apart
(i)	for any reason other than that described in subparagraph (ii), for a period
of not less than three years, or
(ii)	by reason of the petitioner's desertion of the respondent for a period of not
less than five years, immediately preceding the presentation of the petition.
The very simple but complete amendment calls for:
(e) the spouses have been living separate and apart for a period of not less than eighteen months immediately preceding the presentation of the petition.
Basically the hon. member wishes to reduce the period in which spouses have been living separate and apart, either by agreement for three years or by desertion for five years, to 18 months. Within that time the petition providing that evidence would go before a court of a competent jurisdiction whereupon the judge would grant the petition for dissolution of a marriage, provided everything was in order.
It is true that the population of Canada is going up. It is interesting to note that in 1974 in Canada there were 45,019 divorces granted, in 1975 there were 50,611, in 1976 there were 54,207 and in 1977 there were 55,370 divorces granted. In other words, there has been an increase over the four years of approximately 10,000 divorces in Canada. One must look at the sociological changes in reference to why this has occurred.
I believe that one of the causes of tension in a marriage, which has come along with sociological change in Canada and, indeed, in all countries of the western world, is that today, in order to cope with the economic problems, both the man and wife must work. They are, in effect, fenced in as soon as they are married if they buy a home. The cheapest home which can be purchased in Calgary, a 900 square foot bungalow with two bedrooms, costs around $70,000 to $75,000. To meet the down payment couples, particularly young couples, usually have to purchase a first and a second mortgage, harnessing themselves to payments of $700 to $800 per month. This, combined with the high income tax rate in Canada, leaves little left over in their cheques to provide for food and other necessities, particularly if a family comes along. In light of these new economic and social changes which have come about in Canada, the hon. member believes that the law in this regard should be changed.
Parliament is a strange world. In the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs a brief was presented on the treatment of children in this nation and various groups from across the country will be appearing to speak to the proposed bill of rights for children.
I sympathize with the hon. member's position that once a marriage is broken down altogether, it is not much of a life for the people concerned if they have to wait three years or five years for a divorce, so this bill is probably a step in the right direction. If the evidence given before a judge in an undefended divorce case shows that the marriage has irretrievably broken down, then the imposition of any time limit would be a strain on the parties and particularly on children of nine or ten years of age who have to live in that atmosphere. I have had experience of many cases where people lived under such

December 12, 1978

emotional tension, where there was physical or mental cruelty involved, and it is no place for children.
I was impressed with the lady who presented the brief at committee today which pointed out that breakdown in adults was usually the result of what took place in their younger years in their homes or institutions where they lived.
I would be prepared to agree to removing the time provision in the bill and leaving that aspect to the discretion of the judge, or perhaps a time limit of 18 months might be imposed. Once it was obvious the marriage was on the rocks, none of the sanctions of the law would keep people together.
I read some statistics in a newspaper article lately to the effect that one-third of all marriages in Canada end in divorce. That is a rather frightening statistic. When heckling the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore I think the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) said there must be a lot of bad marriages, and I guess that is the problem. Marriage has to be worked at. All of us who have been married know that if people worked as hard at marriage and home life as we do in our occupations, or in our idealistic drive to be in this House, people would stay together.
If the grounds for divorce were extended, that would raise one question for which 1 do not have an answer. It seems to me that people have forgotten their responsibilities toward the children, Mr. Speaker. There are many people in the western world today who did not have children of their own for one reason or another but who adopted children. Many children have found good homes that way and many successful people have come from such homes. I have always reminded adopted children that their parents chose them. They made application, their credentials were checked by people trained and skilled to some degree in child psychology, and they were classed as able to provide a fit home for a child. Unfortunately, many children come into homes where I would not go so far as to say they are not wanted, but they are treated as if they are not wanted.
I would oppose some extensions, Mr. Speaker, but 1 think this one is reasonable. If we have a divorce law, let it be one that works and is practical. People are not helped by having to stay together for a period of three or five years when not only for the spouses involved but for the family the conditions are, if I may put it in plain, ordinary English, hell on earth.
I had an old law partner once who said that lawyers made the worst husbands but they always managed marry very fine women. I feel that I fall into that category and that is a confession I have had to make even in front of my constituents.

speechtext:
Hear, hear!
Mr. Robert Daudlin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary
of State): Mr. Speaker, unfortunately I cannot agree entirely with the two members of the legal fraternity who preceded me. As a matter of fact, I do not know that I could even say "me three" to the confession of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) and the mover of this motion.
I share some of the concerns of those hon. members but I have more difficulty getting over the concept that accessibility of divorce will have little or no effect on the longevity of marriage. I suppose if all of us had the opportunity of legislating good marriage, we would be disposed to legislate what people should do in order to get married rather than how to dispose of marriages once they have gone sour. That is probably what we should be working on.
Given that we have a Divorce Act and given that I was a practitioner of law, as I suppose my friends may have been, when this law came forward, when it was amended and when it took out of existence the "shady lady" divorce we have all heard about, we must bear in mind that at that time there was substantial deliberation on what kind of evidence should be required to demonstrate that a marriage had come to an end. I do not have the law statute as it exists in front of me. However, it seems that what we are saying is that this section of the law states that demonstrable marriage breakdown is evidenced by separation for three years or five years if it is the petitioner petitioning on the basis of his own desertion. If we go to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), if I understood him correctly, time of separation would not be any evidence upon which the court would rely. It would be looking for something else in terms of demonstrating marriage breakdown.

December 12, 1978
Marriage Breakdown
I think that the law which now exists has other categories which set up that kind of indicia of marriage breakdown. In effect, what we were trying to do was to accommodate these people in this section which this bill would amend. We would accommodate those who had nothing in law to put before a court except the fact that the two spouses in a marriage were living separate and apart. That is pretty slim indicia if that is all we are going to give to a judge to administer.
I ask hon. members to consider what happens in a divorce action. I have brought my share before the bar, as I am sure other lawyers here have done. There has been the parade of the parties before the judge, with the judge asking the compulsory questions: Is there a chance for reconciliation? No. How long have you been living apart? Three years. That is fine, and away we go. I have had judges tell me prior to my coming here that if I bring a divorce before that court that is going to take more than three minutes, I obviously have problems with that divorce and it should not be there.
Those would be the same judges upon whose discretion the hon. member for Calgary North would rely to determine, without the indicia of even the three or five years, that in fact there has been a marriage breakdown which would disrupt that very principle to which we are now paying lip service and upon which we say the whole country is founded. That would not satisfy me.
The then minister of justice stated in the House of Commons on October 25, 1976, as reported at page 420 of Hansard', referring to the government:
We will go forward in the immediate future on three aspects relating to family law. The first is negotiations with the provinces toward the establishment in the provinces of unified family courts. The second is changes in the law relating to matrimonial property to better take account of the economic needs and rights of both parties. The third is formal consultation with those in the community across Canada regarding the other recommendations of the Law Reform Commission's report on family law.
These steps were viewed as integral parts of a comprehensive reform of divorce legislation, and in fact steps one and two have now been completed. The establishment in the provinces of unified family courts enables the widest possible number of family law issues attendant on marriage breakdown to be resolved, under our current constitutional framework, in a single court.
As you know, the Law Reform Commission in its 1976 report on family law recommended the establishment of unified family courts. However, the Department of Justice, in response to recommendations made by the Law Reform Commission of Canada in its 1974 working paper on "The Family Court", established a fund to assist interested provinces in developing unified family court pilot projects. Terms and conditions for the department's funding program were approved by Treasury Board in May, 1976. Pursuant to the terms and conditions, a unified family court pilot project is "a project that relates to the development of a unified family court having jurisdiction over a wide range of family matters and including some or all of the following support services:

information and intake services, legal services, investigative services, diagnostic services and enforcement services."
To date the Department of Justice and the attorney general's department in British Columbia are cost sharing the evaluation of a unified family court pilot project that was conducted in the Richmond-Surrey-Delta area of British Columbia. The project was initiated by the provincial government in 1974, and the evaluation report for this project is due shortly.
There is also agreement with the province of Ontario covering the operation of a unified family court pilot project in the city of Hamilton. This project, which will run for three years, was commenced on July 1, 1977, pursuant to provincial legislation establishing this court at the county court level. Negotiations between the federal government and numerous other provinces concerning the establishment of a unified family court pilot project are well advanced, and it is expected that other projects will begin in the near future.
Obviously the federal government cannot establish the courts it wishes in each province as the administration of justice in the province, including the constitution, maintenance and organization of provincial courts, both of civil and criminal jurisdiction and including procedure in civil matters in those courts, is within exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the provinces.
However, this joint federal-provincial approach has resulted in a court which is quite a new concept. The major attribute of these courts is, of course, the unified jurisdiction. Perhaps in no other single area of the law is fragmentation of jurisdiction felt more keenly than in family law. It is for this reason that the unified family courts are presided over by a judge who has not only the jurisdiction traditionally exercised by the provincial family court judge but also the jurisdiction in respect of divorce.
As well as the unified jurisdiction, these courts offer a broad spectrum of dispute resolution techniques. There is a social component complementing the strictly judicial side which seeks to achieve settlement in a non-adversarial fashion to reduce the areas of contention requiring adjudication. Furthermore, these counselling and conciliation services, as they are called, are available not only to spouses in the process of marriage breakdown but also to those who seek to reconcile. Support services aim at preserving and strengthening the family where possible and, where not, attempting to establish a decent workable basis for interspousal transactions such as child custody, property and financial matters.
The Department of Justice continues to maintain the position that the grounds for divorce cannot be isolated from the economic consequences of divorce. Under the existing Divorce Act, economic and custodial bargaining leverage is provided by the requirement of proof of fault, and the availability of fault defences and bars which, if asserted, would preclude the deserting petitioner from obtaining a divorce for a minimum five years. This bargaining leverage helps in many cases to compensate for the laws which may be unfair to the non-wage earning spouse.
December 12, 1978

A transition from fault to no fault divorce grounds and, in particular, a transition that will allow divorce at the request of either spouse after a short waiting period, will render the non-wage earning spouse liable to divorce against his or her will with perhaps unfair financial consequences, at least unless all the traditional common law property systems are adjusted to recognize that the role of homemaker and child rearer is "partnership activity".
I note with some concern that although the proposer of this bill acknowledges this is a problem, he states that since there now appears to be an acceptance of that principle and the adoption of laws in eight of the provinces of Canada, that is adequate and we should be proceeding. If there is one province which has not adopted that kind of law, I say the time is not yet for us to move unilaterally by amendment of this kind to change the kind of leverage I just described. It is for this reason that the Law Reform Commission's recommendations are based on the premise that the concept of fault must be completely eliminated from the whole marriage dissolution process, for example, from grounds, economic consequences and child custody determinations except to the extent that conduct affects reasonable needs or the parent's capacity as a custodian.
Bill C-207 proposes to eliminate the concept of fault from only one ground of divorce by reducing the required three to five-year waiting period to 18 months regardless of the conduct of either spouse. This merely replaces one arbitrary period of time with another. Furthermore it appears to leave the remaining marriage breakdown provisions in section 4 of the Divorce Act intact. Accordingly, somewhat inconsistently, the intention seems to be that a couple could obtain a divorce under section 4(l)(e) by living separate and apart for only 18 months, whereas under section 4(1 )(b), for example, a spouse living separate and apart due to his partner's alcohol or narcotic addiction would be required to wait the full three years. I should add, I suppose, that the hon. member has indicated that he would entertain an amendment that would reduce the requirement to 18 months in all cases. But again, I have serious doubt whether an 18-month period would be long enough. Take a look, for instance, at alcoholism.
Do we despair so much in this society that alcoholism, to use an example, is so irretrievable that a period of 18 months would demonstrate conclusively that it would not be stopped, that it would not be changed, that persons could not change themselves and thus remove themselves from the possibility of divorce purely on that ground? I think not, Mr. Speaker. Time has a way of curing and helping situations like that and should not be a abridged as a result of a bill like this.
It can be suggested that the amendment is not comprehensive and that any divorce reform should await a full reform package which deals with all the grounds. It is regrettable that when a member honestly believes, as I think the hon. member does honestly believe, that the law should be amended as he has indicated, that all hon. members cannot be carried along
Marriage Breakdown
with that same conviction. I have indicated just few of the concerns I have to express with regard to this bill or in terms, even, of any comprehensive change of legislation concerning family breakdown and divorce.
I happen to be completely convinced that the family unit is the basis of the western world's civilization, that it is the basis and the model upon which all hon. members should be patterning and examining laws that we wish to pass in order to determine whether or not they are likely to lead to a better or more just society. I am satisfied that even if inadvertently we make changes that tear apart the fabric of the family unit, directly or indirectly, we will somehow have done a disservice to the nation while attempting to do a service to a few unfortunate individuals who haven't taken the time before entering marriage to consider how permanent and how important an institution they were getting into.

Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in speaking to this bill. It so happens that today is my duty day and I did not even realize that the measure before us was to be discussed. I happened to be in the same position last year when the bill came up and I counted it a privilege to speak on the bill at that time because I think, as the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Daudlin) has said, that marriage is the cornerstone of our society. It is the most fundamental institution we have, and one on which our country is built. Thus, I count it a fortuitous thing for me-perhaps all members will not agree with me but I count it fortuitous- that I was here when the bill came before us.
During the discussion of this bill, which would reduce the waiting period for divorce from three years to 18 months, we have heard from three lawyers in succession. It reminds me of something someone said to me a number of weeks ago. He said that if there was one lawyer living in town he would starve to death, but that if there were two they would both drive Cadillacs. That is the result of the adversary system, Mr. Speaker.
The hon. member for Kent-Essex mentioned the experiment with the family court system which took place in British Columbia. It so happens that the first family court system in British Columbia was set up in my riding of Surrey-White Rock. Obviously, it is under provincial jurisdiction, and includes the municipality of Delta. I want to put on record here that it has been a very successful experiment. I was not speaking entirely in jest when I said that if there was confrontation with two lawyers they would both be driving Cadillacs, because so much of the problem in divorce proceedings is directly related to the adversary system where lawyers are fighting against each other and each is committed to looking after the interest of his client as he sees it. That is how the system is built.
To a large extent the family court system breaks down the adversary system in divorce proceedings. This does not mean all family conflicts will be resolved, but it does mean that one of the elements of conflict is taken out of the process.

Marriage Breakdown
The hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) who introduced this measure has been interested in this subject for a long time by reason of his being a lawyer and because he had to deal with these things, and because he is a family man and is concerned about the family unit. He gave me a lot of support in the promotion of my private member's bill with respect to parental abduction of children, and I will always remember that. But I think it is wrong to try to solve these problems legally or by reducing the waiting period. He was anxious to reduce the waiting period from three years to 18 months and then, after discussion with my colleague from Calgary North, suggested it would not have to be even 18 months, that it could be less-12months-or maybe a shorter period still at the discretion of the judge. It makes one wonder how much this period can be reduced. How far are we willing to go to negotiate the waiting period?
I could not help but think of the days when I was in university taking a course in Russian history. Right after the Russian revolution the leaders in Russia did not believe in the bourgeoise institution of marriage, so they brought in measures for "postcard marriage" and divorce. It was not long, however, before they had to get rid of that system; it became too much for even the bureaucrats to handle. In my view there ought to be ample time for reflection and reminiscence. I remember listening to a marriage counsellor-I hasten to tell hon. members that he was speaking to an audience and not to me personally-Dr. Ticton of Portland, Oregon, a very fine marriage counsellor. He said that all relationships require maintenance. That is a profound statement and one which we tend to overlook.

speechtext:
The hon. members from Saskatchewan can speak flippantly if he likes, but this is a very important subject.
When these starry-eyed young couples come to the altar or to the courtroom and say, "For better or for worse", how long is the "worse" supposed to last? The hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore negotiated with the hon. member for Calgary North and, as he did so, I wondered whether the period was being reduced from three years to 18 months, and then to 12 months, and then still further at the discretion of a judge.
How deep are our interpersonal commitments to each other to be? I believe reducing a waiting period which should serve as a time for analysis, reflection and so forth would be destructive.
The hon. member read into the record a statement from a letter-if I copied it inaccurately, the hon. member can correct me. But this person wrote "when society would be in favour of giving them freedom." What are we talking about-freedom in marriage? Whenever you bring two personalities together you give up some freedom.
It has been said that through divorce there is freedom. When people get married, they bring their personalities into their marriages, but when they go into divorce, they take their

failures with them. There is no such thing as freedom through divorce. That failure haunts people for the rest of their lives.
I am not suggesting that there should not be divorce or that some marriages are not irretrievable. All I saying is that all relationships require maintenance. Perhaps one way to provide the maintenance to which I refer would be to make sure, legally, that a couple contemplating divorce proceedings has adequate time to reflect or to get counselling before taking this action.
I might add that the measure being brought forward seems to run counter to most sociological, criminal, and juvenile trends today. The feeling at the present time is that young people ought to face the consequences of their decisions. This measure implies that we should not have to face up to the consequences of our decisions.
In introducing this bill the hon. member who introduced it called it a matter of divorce reform. I do not think we should use the word "reform" with such ease. When something is referred to as a reform, the implication is that we should agree to it automatically and spontaneously. I am not so sure that a measure like this reform. If we were to adopt this measure, I wonder whether in a few years we would not think it was a retrograde step rather than a reform.
I understand thoroughly the hon. member's motivation for bringing this measure forward. I appreciate the fact that people who have faced the anguish of divorce have come to his office, and he wants to help them. However, I am not convinced that reducing the waiting period from three years to 18 months and ultimately, as the hon. member indicated, having the matter decided judicially, is the proper course so I cannot support this measure.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to Bill C-207 as introduced by the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson), it seems to me one must not overlook the tremendous work performed by the Law Reform Commission with regard to family law, work on which 1 should like to dwell a few moments. As we know, the Law Reform Commission spent over four years studying family law, which enabled it to make recommendations on how to improve, modernize and reform it. Between 1974 and 1976, it published four working papers, the first of which was entitled Family Court, the second, Family Property, the third, Maintenance on Divorce and, finally, the fourth, with which we are concerned today, Divorce.
The reaction to those four working papers, which were published and widely distributed, was generally favourable. The commission subsequently incorporated their basic principles and recommendations in what became known as the Report on Family Law which was tabled in the House on Tuesday, May 4, 1976. The then minister of justice sent copies of that report to all the provincial attorneys general and to the coordinator of family law designated for each province.
December 12, 1978

The recommendations of the Law Reform Commission create in fact an overlapping on the federal legislative authority and their implementation requires a lot of co-ordination and co-operation between both levels of government. Since the tabling of the commission report, the justice ministers and the provincial attorneys discussed at great length the recommendations of the Law Reform Commission and the problems deriving from their implementation.
I shall venture to sum up here the main recommendations contained in the Report on Family Law and the causes of divorce and its economic consequences applying in fact to Bill C-207 which is before us. In the first place, the commission recommended to have a law based on the principle of equality of sexes instead of the present law on divorce. Then, it recommended to eliminate the concept of fault in the process of the dissolution of marriage, namely as far as causes, economic consequences and child custody are concerned, except if that measure would affect the reasonable needs or the capacity of the parents to act as guardians.
You will also remember that the commission recommended the concept of "marriage breakdown", defined as the failure of the personal relationship between husband and wife, which constitutes the only reason of divorce and which is proved conclusively by the evidence of only one of the spouses. The commission also recommended to establish a waiting period of at least six months between the beginning of the process of divorce and the application for a hearing. According to that recommendation, it would not be necessary for the parties to be separated in fact for a minimum period of time before the beginning of the process or the hearing of the petition. When I have concluded my remarks.
The Minister of Justice restricted himself in his speech to dealing with the need for the bill, its implications for parliamentary democracy and federal-provincial relations, and the principles underlying it as the framework for democratic procedure. In my short intervention I should like to draw from reality in showing that in referenda held in other countries we may learn from their experience.
As a parliament, we must lay heavy emphasis on the protection of freedom of individual expression and freedom of association. These two associations are at the centre of parliamentary democracy.
I could go on at great length to prove my point by making reference to the referendum bill of the Parti Quebecois and its defects. Instead, I have chosen to draw from but one example, that of Norway. This quick flashback in history may serve us well in avoiding pitfalls which could befall us. It is my hope this background will prove valuable to all members of the House and the other place. It is true that all of us here are members of parliament, but we represent different political philosophies-Conservative, New Democratic, Social Credit, Liberal, and some of Independent persuasion. But each of us, as a member of parliament, is dedicated to a united Canada. For this reason we have the responsibility of ensuring that Bill
Referenda
C-9 serves as a useful tool of government, that it respects the rights of individual expression and the rights of freedom of association.
Norway had its referendum on entrance to the common market in 1972. The Norwegian referendum was extremely bitter. It divided friends and families. It became sort of an obsession with everyone for months, and it had major lasting political consequences beyond the issue of the referendum itself. In Norway we find that there were umbrella organizations. As in Britain, these umbrella organizations received limited financial support from the government. These yes and no organizations were important, but they did not embrace all political parties or groups.
The "no" campaign in Norway was a true grassroots movement. Independent of the political parties, it developed its own membership of 130,000 active workers in a country of 4 million. In many ways it was composed of the little people, the fishermen, the farmers and workers, who opposed the designs of the elite in Oslo, in the press, and in the political parties. It became bigger than any political party in the country and refused to be taken over by them. The political parties which worked with this movement recognized that the movement was stronger than they were.
Ask yourself, would this bill guarantee the rights of such a grassroots movement? The answer is yes, and that is most important. Would it guarantee its right to operate free from any interference from the political parties? The answer is yes again. These things must be looked at carefully in committee to make sure we do have these kinds of protections in the bill.
We can learn another lesson by looking at the Norwegian example, this time at the "yes" campaign. This was not a grassroots movement like the "no" campaign, but was an umbrella group embracing organized parties, unions, co-operatives and so on. But here we find that the umbrella group had a steering committee which drew mainly from the Labour party and excluded the Conservative party altogether, even though the Conservatives were very strongly in favour of entry. The people running the Norwegian "yes" campaign concluded that it would damage their cause if they were seen to be co-operating too closely with the Conservatives, because the "yes" campaign was mostly concerned with winning supporters of the Labour and Liberal parties who were basically hostile to the Conservatives.
Therefore, on both sides of the coin, it is obvious that without dividing the people into two groups, such as the bill in Quebec might suggest, by not giving the political parties which have different philosophies and different members, an opportunity of representation on their own, we are taking the chance of dealing a terrible blow to the rights of associations, parties, and also of individuals.
We can understand that political parties which agree on a referendum question may still wish to maintain totally separate relations in a referendum campaign. They may agree on the need to vote yes or no, but have very different reasons

December 12, 1978
Referenda
which they wish to advance. The parties may even by extremely hostile to one another on everything but the referendum question.
How does the federal referendum bill approach freedom of association? The answer is simple, and it is the answer you would expect from a Liberal government. Our bill guarantees absolute freedom of association. No party or group would be obliged to cooperate in any way with any other party or group. Every party and group would be able to register independently, to have full rights to collect its own funds, hold its own meetings, and produce its own literature and campaign material.
What is more, our bill recognizes the equal interest of federal and provincial parties in a referendum on constitutional questions and gives them exactly the same rights. We even guarantee that provincial parties will have equal broadcast time with federal parties. Every effort has been taken to ensure that our bill does not favour federal parties over other political groups.
It had been my intention to present a short background which might whet the appetite of hon. members of parliament to participate in committee so that this very useful tool, Bill C-9, an act respecting public referendums in Canada on questions relating to the Constitution of Canada, may be a landmark in our legislative history.
If, in my opening statement, I in any way made any remarks which the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands would consider unparliamentary, she can rest assured that I will review the context and will be very willing to withdraw them. If I have been prompted to say what I have said, it is because, in concluding, I want to bring your attention to the principles of the bill. This is what second reading is all about.
The principles are the following: the procedures governing a referendum should be fully consistent with all those political rights normally respected in Canada, especially freedom of expression and freedom of association; the procedure should impose financial controls which encourage a fair and open debate; the procedure should ensure the probity of the referendum process at the same high level as the probity of the electoral process; the procedure should respect the federal nature of Canada and not favour parties or groups active at the federal level over those active at the provincial level; and, the procedure should be as simple and as familiar as possible.
I look forward to active debate, constructive criticism, and some conflict in committee. I encourage all members of this House to participate fully. We may once again prove that "it is in the heat of conflict that the spark of truth is blown."

Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) knows, I listened very carefully to what he had to say. When I came into the House at eight o'clock I came anticipating that the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) would make a speech
December 12, 1978

the likes of which he made one evening in my company to my Kiwanis club, at my invitation. He will recall that well. I introduced him and listened with great anticipation on that occasion. My anticipation on that occasion was rewarded by not only the quality of the speech but by the way in which it was delivered and the sincerity of its message. I listened for that tonight expecting to hear it from the hon. member. I did not hear it.
Unfortunately, what we heard from the hon. member, who happens to be my friend, was a speech containing references to hon. members of this House which, if not contrary to the rules regarding proper parliamentary practice, certainly bordered on the wrong side. I am glad the hon. member is going to review those matters in relation to the charges he levelled at hon. members in this House of Commons.
One interesting thing about this House of Commons is that I have not come up against a member of the House, regardless of the side on which he or she may sit, who takes a devious or dangerous attitude to the country, or an attitude in respect of the country that is wrong. We may have some differences about leadership, but I am getting sick and tired, quite frankly, of sitting in this House hearing from members on the other side that the country's only salvation is a return of that derelict group which passes itself off as good government. I think that is a matter of truth, spoken in a proper parliamentary fashion. The truth is it has become apparent not just to members of this House, but to people across the country, including those in the riding of the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain.
There are two tragedies in the speech of the hon. member. The first tragedy is that he made the speech at all, and the second tragedy is that he made it after a two-hour adjournment break for dinner when he had time to think about it. I do not know how we can advance the cause of this debate if that is to be the level at which it is to be conducted.
We are dealing with something which is extremely important to the country, as the Minister of Justice himself has said. We are dealing with something which is important and fundamental to the parliamentary process, as the Minister of Justice also mentioned in his speech. Although 1 may disagree in some respects with the Minister of Justice and I may suspect some of the motives of this government, at least the Minister of Justice addressed the question of the role of parliament and its relations to this bill on referenda seriously. 1 do not agree with everything he said, but certainly the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain made a speech which was not worthy to follow the speech of the Minister of Justice.
The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain in his speech made reference to a bill put on the order paper by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) dealing with capital punishment. As I recollect, that bill calls for a referendum on capital punishment. The hon. member for Northumberland-Durham is a private member in this House and has the right to put forth whatever bill he wishes. Members can decide to support it or talk it out, as they see fit. The
Referenda
important thing about that bill in the name of the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham is that it, like every other referendum bill in Canadian history, is directed to a specific point and was not designed, as this bill is capable of being used, to deal with a much broader question.
As I read and listened with great care to the excellent speech made by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), this was one of the problems she had with the bill, not that it dealt with referenda but that if dealt with the subject in a broad way and that in so dealing with it in that sense it could change, if used improperly, the course of parliamentary government as we understand it and as we know it. One of the members of the press gallery commented as I was leaving for dinner hour that it was a good speech. The hon. member said that that question, its effect upon the parliamentary system and where it will lead us in terms of the constitutional position of Canada, should be very carefully considered by this House of Commons and by the committee to which the bill will be eventually referred.
Another concern expressed by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands was that she did not believe that the process of constitutional reform in Canada was such a trivial matter that it ought to be dealt with piecemeal, that there ought to be a bill on referenda, a bill on the power of the Senate, the courts, etcetera, or a bill on how we distribute power. This whole process into which we have entered does not have the complete support of some elements of this country. I do not have to tell members of the government how Senator Eugene Forsey feels, how Senator Daniel Lang feels, or how Senator George Mcllraith feels about this approach to constitutional reform.

Mr. Speaker, the question of whether they passed it is very important, and what is equally important is the majority by which it was passed.
I listened quietly to the Leader of the New Democratic Party defame the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) this afternoon, and I did not interrupt on questions of privilege. I think those overly sensitive people in that party could convince the House and the public a great deal more if they would produce a resolution tonight that says something to the contrary. They will have ample opportunity to do that. It is particularly important that they do it because that party has always prided itself on having the parliamentary wing and the leadership of the party follow the dictates of the annual meeting. However, I remember they did that in Ontario. Stephen Lewis raised the minimum wage after his party had done so and he suffered for it.
It is a well known fact that the Quebec wing of the New Democratic Party has for a long time wanted separate status for the province of Quebec. That is common knowledge. I say that the leader of that party ought not to draw himself up to his full five and one half feet and call himself one of the bastions of confederation. The Minister of Justice and others ought not to look upon this party as particularly good allies in the fight to save Canada, in view of that resolution. I think it is very important to say that, and I say it because this afternoon I heard the leader of that party, who should know better, stand up and misquote, and repeat a misquote of the Leader of the Opposition with respect to his position on national unity. He said that the Leader of the Opposition had indicated that he was prepared to negotiate with respect to the province of Quebec in the sense of the division of this country.

speechtext:
I want this House to know, Mr. Speaker, that that is not the case. The quotation was in La Presse; a recording is available for any hon. member who wants it. This is what he said. The Leader of the Opposition said that the mandate of a Canadian prime minister is to preserve national unity. The Leader of the Opposition is not prepared to negotiate separation. I do not think that other party over there is prepared to negotiate it, nor are we. A referendum in Quebec might affect the mandate of a provincial premier but it could not affect the mandate of a federal prime minister.
There is no way, as the law exists today, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the next prime minister who will take office after the election, or any prime minister of this country has a mandate to negotiate the separation of this country. That is a bottom line of Canadian truism.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, it is the essence of federalism to negotiate with any premier when there is a mutually agreed upon agenda. In this case negotiation would simply emphasize two totally opposite points of view. That is what the Leader of
December 12, 1978

the Opposition said in Quebec. I want to lay to rest once and for all the quote, misquote, and repetition of it which is a malignant statement and contrary to the attitude of the Leader of the Opposition. I think it is time this was said. I thought more of the Leader of the New Democratic Party than that he would stand up in this House and make that dreadful statement. I hope he will see fit to set the record straight.
As far as 1 am concerned, Mr. Speaker, there are no second class Canadians if they honestly believe in this country. There is no parliamentarian in this House who ought not to be concerned about this referendum bill and with respect to the principle of the right of the people to be involved in the fundamental question affecting their country.
The committee will have to deal with this bill as it dealt with Bill C-60, and discuss the propriety of it in the context of the time in which they deal with it and with parliamentary practice. It is not our intention to attempt to deny the committee that power and that right. This bill is as important as Bill C-60 which dealt with a certain aspect of the confederation debate. The government saw fit in those circumstances to send that bill to a special joint committee of this House. I was not a member of the committee, but during the summer I watched the proceedings. It was a fairly constructive committee and it recognized the folly of Bill C-60 in the context of the time- that it was just a bit of a confrontation between the provinces and the other institutions. As a result of pressure from the committee the question of the Senate has been referred to the Supreme Court of Canada because the government felt it had to back off. I think it did so quite appropriately.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands suggested that we should deal cautiously with something that it so fundamental to our parliamentary government, and I support her in that. I think it is regrettable that in matters of this kind the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain and certain other members on that side of the House should try to distort the attitude in the country with respect to referenda. His speech is very unfortunate, in view of the seriousness of the proposal, and I hope that as time goes on he will reconsider his remarks. Those remarks were probably prepared for him by the research office of the government. If that is the case, I forgive him, but this debate is so important it demands more consideration than has been given to it by that hon. member.
I listened carefully to what the Minister of Justice said, and I know his intentions as he expressed it.
This parliament has run its course. We are into the fourth session of an elongated parliament. The government has long since run out its moral mandate and has nearly run out its legal mandate. Therefore this is not the government, whatever its stripe, to trust with the tools for recreating confederation, with regard to this bill. That is my position. I make no apology for it. I hope that will be examined during the course of the debate.
One can imagine the position of this government and the turmoil it is in. The leader of the government faces invidious
Referenda
alternatives. Imagine the effect that has on the leadership. He is faced with being deposed from office by the Leader of the Opposition on the one hand, or by John Turner of Toronto on the other. That is an invidious position.
I do not think we can trust nor should we trust a major departure in a parliamentary sense to a government that is so led and so preoccupied with its own position rather than with those matters which should concern it. I am therefore very concerned about this bill in the hands of the government. When the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands spoke of her concern about this bill and the parliamentary practice, she spoke for a lot of people both inside and outside this House of Commons.
There is one other aspect I want to deal with from a parliamentary point of view. The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain used to be the Liberal party whip. He is now a parliamentary secretary. When he occupied the position of whip, he and I worked together. He took some part in the operation of this House of Commons. I am surprised that he did not at least question the amount of time that will be allowed to debate this bill in the House of Commons.
I do not know whether 40 hours will be sufficient. I do not know how the government can say that 40 hours are sufficient in terms of debate on such an important matter as the question that may face us with regard to the constitution of this country. I do not think we should be fettered in terms of time in dealing with the questions of form and structure. We are not merely talking about an amendment to the family allowances, business corporations act, or even second reading on a bill with regard to referenda. What we are talking about is the opportunity for members of parliament, each of whom represents 125,000 to perhaps 200,000 people, to debate the kind of questions that will be put across this country, not just in one province or even a group of provinces. I hope the government will agree that we not be fettered with regard to time.

The minister is quite right. I repeat, there should not be any fetter with regard to time limitations. There may be two members or a dozen members of this House who will not be able to deal with the bill. I am sure the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain will want to speak on a bill like that. I will want to, as 1 am sure other members will. When the bill goes to committee, I want the government to consider that very carefully.
There are certain remedies which the government has, although I do not believe they should be used on such a bill. I would not want to see the remedy of allocation of time. There was a free vote on the issue of capital punishment, and properly so, and every member was permitted to speak his mind on that moral issue. Whether we agreed with one another is not important. What was important was that every member was given time.
A matter that may affect the preservation of this country and the position the federal government should take on certain matters is worthy of the same kind of consideration as the

December 12, 1978
Referenda
capital punishment issue. I ask the Minister of Justice to consider that. We should not move hastily on this matter. We should move properly and with certainty, and with the knowledge that the people of Canada will understand precisely this whole issue.
Those are my concerns with regard to this bill. I have said in other places that I am not personally opposed and that I have no strong feelings against the principles of the referendum. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands indicated in her speech today that she was not opposed to the idea of referenda. However, she is concerned about the scope of this one because of its importance to the preservation of confederation as we understand it, or the confederation which it might evolve.
All members are concerned about this in terms of our country. I am sure there is not one member of parliament who is prepared to give one inch in connection with the maintenance of confederation in Canada. I wish that debate would end in this House of Commons. 1 worry when it continues. I worry about attacks and misquoting of political leaders. An attack was made today on the Leader of the Opposition. I have never attacked the Prime Minister on anything he has said about the preservation of this country. I have done that as a matter of principle. I hope that is the kind of atmosphere that will prevail when this bill goes to committee.
In conclusion, I am not at all opposed to new parliamentary forms. All I want is for those forms to be considered. I am not opposed to strong government in this country. The parliamentary system demands strong government. On the other hand, I want this parliament to be place where that strong government and its servants must account. After these important issues have been discussed, I would like the bill to go to committee where it can be discussed completely.
I would rather this matter were considered as part of a constitutional package. I do not have that luxury, except to say that is what I would like. However, the government has decided that is not going to happen. When something involves not only this parliament but the federal and provincial institutions, it should be considered as part of an over-all constitutional package.
I hope that in the last few moments I have indicated the spirit with which I and my party view this bill. It would be better to discuss the merits of this bill rather than the merits of each other, because this is an important piece of legislation.
