Mr. Speaker, I don't think that the sheer size of a man is a true measure of his greatness but rather the kind of head he has on his shoulders. In the regard Mr. Speaker, I wonder what is the policy of the Progressive Conservative party on the subject matter of Bill C-9. Indeed, it is extremely difficult of anyone who listened to the speeches made by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), to know what is the position of that party on the issue of the Referendum Act. What is extremely difficult to explain, Mr. Speaker, is the inability of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton to defend his leader after it was twice suggested here in the House of Commons that he would negotiate his country if 60 per cent of people voted yes in a Quebec referendum.
Some people bury their heads in the sand, and when they come to the province of Quebec-it is extremely important in this country-they know that people outside of Quebec do not listen to them as much because they use French, and therefore they feel they can say any silly things. They may try to make the people of Quebec believe something. The next day they fly to another part of the country where they say exactly the opposite. They are certain that nobody will contradict them. They believe there are in Canada people who do not understand both languages. There are others, Mr. Speaker, who, in their wishful thinking, believe they live in a unilingual country. They think because they speak in some way in Quebec they will not be understood elsewhere, and because they speak in some other way in the provinces they will not be understood in Quebec. They are understood just the same, Mr. Speaker; furthermore, they will always be understood. I think the important thing-Mr. Speaker, to my knowledge, and it does not seem a long time for some members or perhaps too long for a few, but the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands has made the worst speech 1 have ever heard in the House. I do not claim to be the official critic of a party but I can say at least, Mr. Speaker, that I can recognize when somebody has the future of his country at heart, because the bill before us is extremely important for the future of our country.

December 12, 1978
Referenda
We have not introduced this piece of legislation, Mr. Speaker, solely to while away the time in the House, we introduced to guarantee the very foundations of our democratic society in Canada. What we want to do with Bill C-9, Mr. Speaker, is to guarantee to the Canadian people as a whole that no government will be able to usurp or to break this country unfairly. When we say unfairly, Mr. Speaker, we want to ensure that those who were elected in Quebec through the democratic process do not break this country in a way which would clearly be antidemocratic. I will explain this way. What I mean, Mr. Speaker, is that it would be extremely easy for a party which forms the government to try to deceive the population on the terms of the question. 1 believe it would be evidence of political immaturity for the federal government to evade its responsibilities by not introducing a legislation such as Bill C-9.
Mr. Speaker, we are not introducing a bill on referenda strictly for the fun of it. We introduce this bill to make sure that if ever the group of bourgeois who are in power in Quebec decide to fool around with the meaning of the referendum question we could redress the wrong that would have been done and we could know, clearly and accurately, whether Quebeckers want to remain within Canada or not. 1 believe there are hon. members in this House who have yet to understand that the future of Canada is at stake right now, in 1978, and not in six years or ten years from now. Too many members on the other side of this House are prepared to endanger their own country for the sake of power. 1 do not understand them, Mr. Speaker. It is maddening to see how these people refuse to understand the problem which now exists in Canada. It is shocking to note how these people prefer to destroy the will of the House of Commons that wants to try to keep Canada united through the present government which represents people from all parts of the country. Mr. Speaker, it is extremely difficult to understand how come these people, after what we heard tonight and after so many years in the opposition, have not learned anything yet. I think they are now a permanent opposition party. They have not learned yet to listen to the grass roots. That is what is important. These people, Mr. Speaker, have not realized what a Quebecker wants at all costs to stay within Canada. They do not take the trouble.
Mr. Speaker, they should take the trouble to look into the underlying principles of Bill C-9, particularly on the matter of referendum procedures. These were dealt with in a very superficial way. With all the experience of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, I would have expected from him a much better worked out speech on this bill.
Mr. Speaker, to my mind there is no serious awareness of the real urgency of having a referendum act in this country, an act that would enable us to ensure that democracy is safeguarded in Canada. Mr. Speaker, I hear voices on the other side. Unfortunately they know nothing about the way the party in power in Quebec communicates. If they think as some do, that Quebeckers can be bought off when they cannot speak
the way Quebeckers want to be spoken to, well, they will miss the boat, Mr. Speaker. And in the House of Commons they will have, many will be missing, namely the representatives of Quebec. Then they will wonder whether the House of Commons can survive after that. There might even be a House of American representatives in our area.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is imperative that those people become aware, once and for all, that all the Quebec people want is simply that their problems not be made light of, that they be solved. Quebeckers want nothing more. They also want something that is basic. I feel that, humanly speaking, if French Canadians are truly respected, then, it should be understood that the French language should be respected throughout the country. When we can finally tell Quebeckers that you, on the other side, have a deep respect for them, then there will be no more problems in Canada. But Quebeckers are not convinced, Mr. Speaker, that people on the other side want them in Canada. On the contrary, a good number of them wonder if people like the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton would not simply want them to opt out. Unfortunately, they already see themselves in power. Were it not for us in Quebec, they might be in power. Those guys are ready to negotiate their country for power. Mr. Speaker, I will not dwell on them any longer. I would rather speak of the bill, which is more important and more sensible.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to summarize the bill which to me is extremely important. The Quebec premier, Mr. Levesque, incidentally is my MLA, I did not vote for him, but he won his election anyway. Mr. Speaker, the Quebec premier said that our referendum legislation was "full of holes", nothing but holes. I will show him, Mr. Speaker, what has more holes.
I would like to make 19 points, 19 comparisons between the Quebec legislation and the bill before us this evening. After that, let him try and find holes! Anyway we are going to find some.
Mr. Speaker, according to Bill C-9, referenda should only deal with constitutional matters. The Quebec legislation says that referenda may deal with any matter, but there could not be more than one referendum on the same subject during the same legislature. They are ready to do anything to gain power. They said that they had a taste for Quebec, but now they have a taste for power, Mr. Speaker.
Second point. We are making quite clear, Mr. Speaker, after the answer given this afternoon by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde), that the referendum would be held for consultation purposes only. In their legislation they say that a referendum might be held for consultation purposes or to submit to the people a bill passed by the National Assembly before its final approval. So they pass a legislation but they consult the people before giving it their final approval. They are putting the cart before the horse.

December 12, 1978

Third point, Mr. Speaker. Let us not forget that the Quebec Premier said that our bill was full of holes. We say that the questions asked in a referendum could only be worded by a government member, at least by the entire cabinet. If you look at the legislation, Mr. Speaker, it is characteristic of the bourgeois clique that runs the show in Quebec; only the premier could word the questions put in a referendum. When the leader says jump everybody agrees and the others have nothing to say.
Such is the basic democracy they talk about in Quebec.
The next point-I go on with the bill full of holes, according to the Quebec Premier. The questions should be worded so as to allow the voters to answer yes or no, which does not exclude the possibility to ask several questions, including alternative questions. He forgets this himself!
Mr. Speaker, I would not like to sound like a Social Crediter, as I have much more respect for them than for those people, but if I went further, they have been bothering us for a long time with their famous question. That is dangerous. Mr. Speaker, there is a way to ask the question which I think is very, very important. I have nothing against people who have spent years at the university, who have studied for a long time and who have been teachers. We find a lot of those people as in the Parti Quebecois but all things considered, they should put more trust in Quebeckers. I get fed up that in Quebec, Mr. Speaker, only academics dominate people who are working hard, when the others spend their time deciding and governing. Therefore the question which will be put will be very important, and skilful as they are at manipulating crowds they believe that Quebeckers are stupid people. That will be their biggest mistake.
Recently there was a public opinion poll held in Laval, a prosperous city with a dynamic mayor. He had decided once and for all that he would not be ruled by fascists because if you do not think as the government party does you are a bad but you are okay if you share their views.
Mr. Speaker, to come back to what I have to say, housewives from Laval have clearly indicated according to the last poll they are sick and tired, and that is only a few Quebeckers who are tired of being manipulated by a sort of question which will result in a "yes" or a "no". They want to know clearly what the question will be.
And if you try to manipulate the people by presenting them with a leading question, they will come out with a loud and clear "no" as an answer to the question whether or not they want Quebec to separate.
I now would like, Mr. Speaker, to point out the shortcomings in our legislation by comparison to that of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, we are ready to grant forty hours for the consultation process to take place and when a referendum is held, they will grant thirty hours. We will not press the point for the sake of ten hours and I guess that democracy is all the more respected when more people can have more time to express their views.
Secondly, what we are saying is that after the wording of the question has been approved, the government will only have
Referenda
45 days to issue writs for the referendum. Pursuant to its act, the government of Quebec will not be able to issue any writs until the twentieth day following the day when the phrasing of a question has been approved but it could also delay the issuing of that writ indefinitely. That is their way of understanding democracy, Mr. Speaker. The Quebec government will not be able to issue a brief during the yearly census period or the two following weeks. That is the Parti Quebecois' idea of democracy, Mr. Speaker! We can also see it at work, Mr. Speaker, in its occupational safety program. They are taking away all the benefits workers have enjoyed up to now, as far as the safety is concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few additional remarks but first I would like to make a very important point. I did not seek legal advice nor do I pretend to be a lawyer, far from it, but I am seriously wondering whether I or any of my hon. friends opposite, from the left to the right, will be allowed to write to our constituents during the referendum campaign to let them know our position and feelings on that matter or whether we will have to and I do mean "have to" become part of an umbrella organization before expressing our views.
Mr. Speaker, I think this is extremely important and if you have time one day you might study this bill in order to determine if it does not violate our privileges as members. If we examine the Quebec referendum legislation we notice that any organization wanting to contribute during the referendum campaign must either be in the "yes" or "no" umbrella group. If we stick to the text, this means that the member for Longueuil is not authorized to write to his electors and advise them to vote no. And also that during the whole referendum campaign members of this House will not have the right to go and speak to people in Quebec in order to convince them to stay in Canada if they are not in the umbrella group. That is what the legislation means in Quebec now.
Mr. Speaker, I find this extremely dangerous. What is sure in my mind is that I have been elected to represent people who believe in that kind of country and that the government party will not prevent me from holding public meetings in which I can express my point of view and explain why I want to keep my country as it is. If they think I am doing something illegal, Mr. Speaker, they can send me their thugs if they want to.
Mr. Speaker, it is extremely dangerous for a society which calls itself democratic to start invading rights and privileges of some members of parliament. And that is when you really see what the federal system is all about when whatever level of government unilaterally decides to attempt reducing the rights of some individuals, the other level can interfere to stand for them while if we had a separation such as the one provided for by the Parti Quebecois group, we would refer to one single government in Quebec, under a presidency, how do I know, such as they have in France with their communes or whatever, and all the frills around it, when one looks at it it is beyond understanding.
Mr. Speaker, it is both extremely dangerous and important to point out the reasons for Bill C-9 now before us. If members

December 12, 1978
Referenda
in this House, and I would invite them to listen closely, if members are to be restricted in their right to speak or hold public meetings in support of Canada in the province of Quebec during the referendum campaign, without being a member of the yes group or the no group, it is extremely dangerous for our Canadian society and our Canadian democracy to let this go unchallenged. Things are happening in Canada where one part does not give a damn about the other. What is happening in Canada? Some people believe that because a dreamer or a saviour has come, the other side's problems are solved. Mr. Speaker, the problem is much deeper. If ten, twelve or fifteen members of all sides decided during the pre-referendum campaign or the referendum campaign in Quebec to hold public meetings for a united Canada, it would be interesting to find out whether we would have the right to do so.
Mr. Speaker, under the legislation that was passed in the province of Quebec, members would not have the right to do so. They would have that right if they were to join the yes umbrella, and we know what it means to join the yes umbrella. I am quite ready to associate myself with the provincial Liberal party, but let us not forget that the communist party also supports them. It is against separation. Therefore, I would have to associate with the communists.
Well, I would not suggest for a moment that the New Democratic Party are communists. In my view, they are socialists, albeit bourgeois socialists. They are intellectuals controlling workers and taking their funds for electioneering. This is what they are doing. A great leader once said they were Liberals in a hurry, but as far as I am concerned I feel they are backwards on a number of things. When we look at the principles and the main provisions in the legislation before us, the clear realization is that we have a responsible government.
I should like to mention some provisions of Bill C-9 which I feel are the most important, although I have already mentioned a number of others. First of all, referenda should deal only with constitutional issues. They could be part of an advisory process. The answers to the questions would be an unequivocal yes or no. The referendum legislation would expire at the end of a five-year period, unless parliament decided otherwise. Our referenda could be held either in a designated area or at the same time in a few designated areas or everywhere in Canada. As I indicated earlier, the consultation process on a definite question would last 40 hours. As to the writs, 45 days would be required. The bill provides also for a judicial recount in cases where the results are very important and the number of "yes" and "no" votes are too close. Mr. Speaker, the reason I fully support the underlying principle of this bill-something hon. members opposite will or can not understand-is that its purpose is to safeguard the democratic process in Canada. And I have a lot of respect for those who do not think that way, Mr. Speaker, but I say one thing, they did not consider at length the problem that exists in Canada.
If the separatist party in power in Quebec said clearly our question is going to be so clear that people are going to be able
[Mr. Olivier.)
to answer yes or no, that our question is going to be: Do you want to remain in Canada, yes or no, there would probably be no need to introduce this bill immediately. That is what is important. There are fundamental reasons why the Parti Quebecois keeps postponing its proposed referendum. First of all, everyone knows that they are scared to death of the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau). They know that on his own ground which is the province of Quebec, Mr. Rene Levesque is going to go down to defeat. And they know also that when the people of Quebec are going to be called upon to make a choice between Rene Levesque and Pierre Elliott Trudeau, the answer is going to be 70 per cent for Mr. Trudeau. They know that. Twenty per cent will be undecided and 10 per cent will be for Mr. Levesque-and I am being generous.
Mr. Speaker, I will never draw enough the attention of this House to the problem of our democracy that is at issue in Quebec and in Canada because of the umbrella organizations because members of the House will probably not have the right to speak during the referendum process if they are not members of the umbrella organizations. That is extremely important. Although I seldom share the opinions of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, I think she has the right to say what she has to say in my riding, in my province, in my city or in her city-everywhere. I think it is normal, even if I do not think like her. But 1 say one thing, I believe she has not yet understood that she will not be able to do so during the referendum period in Quebec unless she is part of the umbrella organization. I find that extremely odd, Mr. Speaker.
There are some who seem to say that the Liberal party is in trouble. I challenge them to come and see what is happening in Quebec. Because we stand for the people of Quebec, because Liberal members elected to Ottawa stand for the interests of Quebec and always do so energetically, they imagine that we cannot understand the other problems that exist in this country. But the important thing in this bill, Mr. Speaker, is to help all hon. members from the province of Quebec and the members of all parties in the House and place them in a position where they can take part in an honest debate on the desire of a population to remain part of the country. There are too many people in the House, Mr. Speaker, who figure the future of the country is a matter of dollars and cents. This country will never make it as a united country if people, be they in the Liberal party, in the Progressive Conservative party, in the Social Credit party or in the New Democratic Party, believe that we will make friends with those who oppose the idea of a united Canada by pretending it is strictly a matter of economic problems. It is not so. We will never solve Canada's problems by talking about dollars and cents. Never! The problem will disappear when people start respecting those who come from Quebec, be they French-speaking or English-speaking. There is a French-speaking majority in Quebec. There is an important minority in Canada which demands to be respected like other Canadians living outside Quebec. And as long as people fail to understand this problem, Mr. Speaker, it will not be
December 12, 1978

solved in Canada. On the contrary, they will still manage to split and divide this country. Mr. Speaker, I conclude by saying that with Bill C-9 we cannot be certain of winning the referendum, because we are sure that the party in power in Quebec, the Parti Quebecois, will lose the referendum. I tell you one thing; be careful, you are dreaming in colour. A growing majority of Quebeckers think that the other provinces do not want them anymore. I tell you one thing, Mr. Speaker, to believe that the referendum will automatically be rejected in Quebec is to dream in colour. I tell you one thing, Mr. Speaker, if there were a referendum in the Longueuil riding tomorrow morning, if we asked the question yes or no, do you want to stay in Canada, I am not sure Canada would win. The population in Longueuil, Mr. Speaker, is 93 per cent Frenchspeaking, 8 per cent English-speaking, and 4 per cent immigrants. Mr. Speaker, this is really significant. People on the other side think it is easy to be a member of parliament in Ottawa. If you believe it is easy to be a member of parliament in Ottawa when you are from Quebec you are mistaken. You should come in our ridings where we are always defending ourselves, where one keeps repeating that the Parti Quebecois is not telling the truth, that it is not true that English-speaking people are out to get us, that it is not true that they want to destroy us, that it is not true they are this and that. When you come to do this work for us, I will begin to have some respect for you.

subtopic: NATIONAL FILM BOARD-REASONS FOR CHANGES TO FRENCH REGIONALIZATION PROGRAM
NATIONAL FILM BOARD-REASONS FOR CHANGES TO FRENCH REGIONALIZATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the French regionalization program of the National Film Board was established in 1974. There are four regions under this program: Western Canada, Ontario, Quebec, which already has the head office of the NFB, and the region of Acadia. English regionalization has existed longer and is supported by stronger budgetary considerations and better equipment.
In the French sector, in four years, 78 films have been produced. At the head office, since the establishment of the NFB in 1939, only about 30 films we produced outside Quebec which concerned more or less directly French-Canadian realities. This makes .75 films a year for the central operation while regionalization produced 19.5 films a year. This proves the value of the French regional program and the enormous human and technical potential which has not yet been developed. Must I remind the House that, under its terms of reference, the NFB must undertake and promote the production and distribution of films in the national interest, and especially make Canadians more familiar with Canada in addition to promoting knowledge of Canada abroad?
I should also like to tell the minister that French regionalization has generated funds outside the budget of the NFB. I would like to note especially that provincial governments, social clubs, municipal governments and French-Canadian organizations throughout the country have shown an interest in these films. They succeeded in interesting and involving the citizens of the regions and their representatives in local productions. Nor is there any price put on the contribution of volunteer workers who may at times be in short supply in Montreal but certainly not in the regions. It is difficult to measure the impact of a so-called regional film on the rest of the country, but one cannot question its spontaneousness, its originality, its openness and its intrinsic value. A regional film is also less costly to produce in the field in my region than in Montreal or by Montreal based NFB producers.
Adjournment Debate
The suppression of western and Ontario regionalization programs is not a saving but an unfortunate and incalculable loss. Yet regionalizations follow more closely the mandate which is to make Canada known to Canadians. Besides striking a foul blow to French: speaking minorities of the country, the NFB will contribute to further weaken them by taking away from them tools of expression and communication. It is a denial of the most significant part of the NFB mandate in the political context now prevailing in the country. And yet the June 26, 1976 issue of Quebec city's Le Soleil mentioned the comments of NFB commissioner Andre Lamy. Speaking on regionalization, he said, and I quote:
We want to avoid forcing people to work with groups of strangers from Montreal, or uprooting them by forcing them to come to Montreal to produce their films.
And he added:
I want to know what a Canadian from Vancouver thinks, and I want the federal government to give him the means to produce a cultural work that can be made known in Quebec.
And I add, in New Brunswick, Ontario and everywhere else in Canada. Those fine words, those noble feelings, that generous condescension are no longer valid today.
The country is moving openly towards the right and seems ready to sacrifice minorities and this in the midst of a national crisis. Principles and fine speeches are easily forgotten. For the sake of budget restrictions, a very nasty discrimination is practised, Mr. Speaker. If we do not take care, such discrimination will give rise to a more radical militancy than what we have seen up to now among minorities. I did say discrimination and I will give evidence based on figures and facts. The following are the cuts made by the NFB in the regionalization item of the 1979-80 budget. For English production, including the Pacific coast, the prairies, Ontario and the Atlantic region, no section has been abolished and the budget has been reduced by only $50,000. On the other hand, for the French production, the western and Ontario centres have been closed. They are merely abolished and the cut is $340,000.
There is a "proportional"-between quotation marks, not mine, they originate from the official source-reduction of $45,000 in the budget of French regionalization in Quebec. It is obvious that the French regionalizations have hit unduly hard.
This evening I urge the minister or his spokesman to give immediate instructions and put an end to that disgrace. Surely there are other cuts which could be made at the NFB. The hopes of French Canadians living outside Quebec should no longer be frustrated. There should be no more response to the cry-babies of the right. They should stop bleeding minorities drop after drop. The matter I raise goes much further than a mere dollar sign. On behalf of the government and in the face of his commitments towards language minorities, the Secretary of State cannot and should not let the National Film

Board decide unilaterally who will live in French in Canada and where his or her culture will survive.
The regions are fed up with the professionals in Toronto, Ottawa or Montreal who dictate their conditions to the regions as far as their cultural life is concerned. The French regionalizations in western Canada, Ontario and Acadia are cinemato-graphically and culturally viable provided they are not tripped when they begin to walk. The National Film Board has no right to deal so abruptly with the matter of the very existence of the minorities. Furthermore, the regions refuse to see film makers from Montreal come and try to interpret regional realities. Montreal and everything that swarms and scribbles there has never interpreted or has at least misinterpreted Canadian reality in the past. Let us leave that task to the people in the regions. They have begun to do so at CBC, in spite of some weaknesses; let us also do it at the National Film Board. This is an urgent matter, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Daudlin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: NATIONAL FILM BOARD-REASONS FOR CHANGES TO FRENCH REGIONALIZATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for having brought to the attention of the House, and particularly my minister, the problem he brings before us again this evening. He has indicated there have been budget cuts and that there is no department, and no agency under departments that has not been touched by these reductions.
What has been made clear, and 1 will repeat it again this evening, is that the same percentage of funds which has been available for French language productions will continue to be available. The reductions which have taken place are applied to administration costs throughout the country to be sure that the amount of money available for productions will not be reduced by the budget cuts, which had to be applied to this particular area within the department, along with the others.
The French language regionalization program will continue to exist, and its objective will continue to be to show through film the way of life of Francophone minorities outside Quebec. The closing of the Toronto and St. Boniface operations will result in a saving of the administrative and training costs involved, and the resources remaining will be concentrated in order that professional French-speaking film-makers in regions outside Quebec may continue to produce films under this program. While I am not downplaying the seriousness of these cuts and the concerns of those groups affected, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the National Film Board is attempting to ensure that with limited resources the French regionalization program will be maintained.
However, as a result of the comments and projections which have been made by hon. members when bringing this matter to the attention of the minister, he wishes me to convey his assurances that he will continue to consider the program. In addition, he will continue to review what is being done to ensure that the undertakings he has given with respect to the continuance of these programs will be carried out and will not

be drastically affected. Only administrative cuts will result from the budget reductions.

VETERANS AFFAIRS-TRANSFER OF HOSPITALS TO JURISDICTION OF PROVINCES-EFFECT ON VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I questioned the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) with respect to complaints I had received concerning veterans gaining entry to former veterans hospitals which have been transferred to the jurisdiction of the provinces. There have been several news articles recently dealing with this subject.
Two recent cases are causing concern, Mr. Speaker. One concerns the Sunnybrook Hospital, and the other is the Memorial Pavilion, Victoria, British Columbia where veterans were refused access. By the time the respective patients gained entry into another hospital the opportunity for possible effective care had passed and they died shortly afterward. The minister explained there were extenuating circumstances with respect to the Memorial Hospital in Victoria and that the widow had not made proper application. But he said that he knew nothing of the Sunnybrook Hospital situation where veterans have been unable to gain entry. I find it very strange to hear him say that he knows nothing of the Sunnybrook incident.
As official opposition critic for veterans affairs, Mr. Speaker, I call upon the minister to launch an immediate investigation into the problems experienced by veterans in gaining admission to transferred hospitals and to report back to the House as soon as possible.
This afternoon the minister assured us that things were working very well. Well, there is certainly some doubt here, and there is obviously a breakdown in communication when it comes to explaining to veterans how they may gain admission to these hospitals.
I am sure the minister is just as concerned as we are. We want all veterans' needs to be properly met. There have been some very disturbing newspaper articles regarding veterans experiencing difficulties gaining entry into veterans hospitals. A recent article in the Toronto Sun carried the headline "Dying man shuttled by hospitals". The article appeared in the Sun on November 24, and it read in part as follows:
A dying man was shuttled back and forth between three Metro hospitals with no free beds, for eight hours the day before he died, a coroner's jury was told yesterday.
The jury was investigating the Aug. 25 death of Douglas Phillips, 61, of Unionville. He died of a stroke suffered Aug. 24.
"You wouldn't treat a dog like this," his widow Patricia said, describing her horrified reaction Aug. 24 when Sunnybrook Hospital attendants ignored her pleas to help her sick husband-then returned him untreated to Scarborough Centenary Hospital.
In another article on this inquest, printed in the Toronto Star of December 6, we find the following:
December 12, 1978

The jury was investigating the case of Douglas Phillips, 61, who died of a stroke Aug. 25 after two Metro hospitals, Scarborough Centenary and Sunny-brook Medical Centre, refused to admit him. Hospital officials had said there were no beds available.
There definitely is a problem, and the minister's assurances this afternoon that there are no problems and that everything is working fine are completely false.
In the Toronto Star of November 25 we read the following:
There were 108 empty beds at Sunnybrook Medical Centre the night that fatally ill stroke victim Douglas Phillips was refused admittance, his inquest heard yesterday, but not one was in a part of the hospital that could have given him adequate care.
Testimony that concluded yesterday showed Phillips was turned away from Sunnybrook because Dr. John Edmeads, head of neurology, found that every bed in neurology, neurosurgery and internal medicine was booked.
The 61-year-old veteran had wanted to go to Sunnybrook, which Edmeads said has an international reputation and the only stroke unit in Canada-
But still he was shuttled from hospital to hospital. Another headline in the Toronto Star of November 27 states: " 'Shoot me', begged dying man hospitals rejected". What must veterans, who are entitled to entry into veterans hospitals, and their families be thinking when they read headlines like that?
The story reads in part as follows:
A stroke victim-bounced from hospital to hospital due to a bed shortage- pleaded with his wife, "Shoot me. I'm dying," an inquest was told yesterday.
Contrary to the statements made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs this afternoon, all is not well for veterans who try to obtain entry to veterans hospitals. We have a very serious problem on our hands. The inquest was further told that Mr. Phillips died of massive bleeding within the brain. It was termed the "worst kind of stroke." The inquest was told that an ambulance had taken him from his home to Scarborough Centenary where he was assessed as stable, and transferred, at his request, to Sunnybrook Hospital. But Sunnybrook, which had no available beds, refused to accept him. He was left on a stretcher in the emergency ward for more than three hours, and then sent back to Centenary Hospital. That certainly must not be very comforting news for our veterans and their families.
With regard to the hospital on Vancouver Island, problems were identified there over two years ago by the Veterans' Rights Association of British Columbia. Briefly, that association stated:
On behalf of our membership we would like to make you aware of the problems created for veterans on Vancouver Island through the operation and administration of the former Veterans Hospital in Victoria.
That was in a letter sent to all members of parliament. I read this into the record in the House over two years ago and in committee, and I was told that there was no problem at all. Apparently the problem still exists today.
In an article which appeared in the Daily Colonist dated December 8, it is stated:
The Trudeau government failed a Victoria veteran of the two world wars in his hour of greatest need, his sorrowing widow says-
Mrs. Hancox-
Adjournment Debate
That is the wife of the victim,
-said she and her husband had believed beds would always be available for veterans at the hospital. "He believed until almost the end that veterans would be looked after by their country."
We all expected and thought that would happen, Mr. Speaker, so I am asking the parliamentary secretary to give us a firm commitment tonight that there will be immediate investigation and they will report back to the House as soon as possible.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilbert Parent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-TRANSFER OF HOSPITALS TO JURISDICTION OF PROVINCES-EFFECT ON VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to reply to the comments made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) concerning hospital treatment for veterans. He has referred specifically to two recent cases, one occurring at Sunnybrook Medical Centre in Toronto and one at the Royal Jubilee Hospital in Victoria. The hon. member has asked that we give him assurances that these cases will be investigated.
The information regarding the case at Sunnybrook is incomplete at this time, but I will be pleased to inform the hon. member when I have more information. The minister has already spoken briefly about the case in Victoria and I want to reaffirm that, to our knowledge, no refusal of service occurred.
The hon. member made reference to the time a few years ago when there were some complaints at the Victoria Hospital. I can tell him that I personally, as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, visited the Royal Jubilee Hospital at Victoria, was shown around the premises, and had extensive discussions with many of the doctors and nurses. It is obvious to me from the information I received when I was there that the problems, which were seemingly prevalent a few years ago when the letter which the hon. member read into Hansard was written, have now been resolved.
The government recognizes and accepts its moral responsibility to provide the best possible care for our veterans. Over the years, the number of veterans requiring acute and active care has steadily declined, for obvious reasons. Most of the patients in veterans hospitals required chronic or domiciliary care, and this led to difficulties in maintaining and attracting the type of highly qualified medical and support personnel to which we had become accustomed. To overcome this situation it was decided that services could be kept at a high level by integrating our facilities and patients into the total community medical hospital complex. This can best be accomplished when the facilities come under provincial jurisdiction.
Transferring a facility to a province does not represent the end of our responsibility for the care of the veteran patient. Guarantees are provided by the province in each case that a specified number of beds is to be made available for the sole use or priority use of veterans. The provinces have consistently honoured these commitments. I can assure the hon. member of this particular aspect.
Further, in each region of the country a departmental medical officer is employed to assist in assessing the veterans'

Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a question, and then a supplementary question, about the possible commitment of our troops to Namibia. My question was fairly simple, and the supplementary equally simple. Perhaps I could quote parts of both of them. My question ended as follows:
-will the government now undertake to bring a resolution before the House for debate before a final decision is made to send troops on a new and major UN commitment?
My supplementary question ended as follows:
Can the Prime Minister assure the House that we will have an opportunity to debate a resolution in this House on this important matter?
As the Prime Minister likes to do when faced with a question which he does not enjoy answering, he shifted the premise. In his first answer he indicated that he thought they had the support of the opposition in peacekeeping operations, where Canada is indeed in the forefront of all countries. He shifted over to talking about peacekeeping, instead of indicating whether we had a commitment. In answer to the supplementary question, he shifted over to whether there was a commitment made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson).
Was there a commitment or was there not? The Prime Minister denied it twice. He said:
All the Secretary of State for External Affairs said was that if the United Nations asked us for further troops, we would naturally consider the request.
Further on he said:
To my knowledge, there is no commitment. The Secretary of State for External Affairs made no commitment.
On November 28, 1978, as reported in the proceedings of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said the following:
I have said before this committee on a previous occasion, and repeated, that if a force is established, if the circumstances are satisfactory in so far as we are concerned we would certainly be prepared to participate because, of course, we have been one of the architects of this effort and it would be quite inconsistent with that approach not to go on to the next logical step.
Whether there was a commitment is not the main reason I raised this question tonight. Will the government make a commitment to bring this matter before the House of Commons before it sends troops overseas, or before it takes final steps to agree to send our troops to Southwest Africa?
There are a number of precedents for this, but I should like to refer to only four. One was in 1956, at the time of the Suez crisis, when Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Pearson agreed to the

sending of troops and agreed to bringing it before the House of Commons. In 1960, at the time of the Congo matter, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was the prime minister. He brought it before the House of Commons in the form of a resolution before sending troops to the Congo. In 1964, at the time of the Cyprus matter, Mr. Pearson was the prime minister and Mr. Martin was the secretary of state for external affairs. They brought it before the House of Commons.
It is interesting that in the debate on February 19, 1964, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, the present hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), asked a question very similar to the one I directed to the Prime Minister the other day. In those days the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson was the prime minister, and he said the following:
Finally, if a request is made involving the use of substantial numbers of Canadians abroad, we would bring the matter before parliament before any final decision is taken.
It was quite simple. They knew the role of parliament. They were all willing to bring it before parliament, although at the time of the Suez crisis it was post factum by some six days. But the Liberal government of that day had to recall parliament to do it, which was the reason for the six-day delay. It recalled parliament to have it approve the dispatch of troops to the Suez.
Right up until the present Prime Minister it had always been considered the role of parliament to have a veto over such a decision, and that the government by itself could not commit our troops abroad in any major new undertaking. I do not know whether we should consider this matter as peacekeeping. I did not use the word "peacekeeping". The Prime Minister, looking for a fresh subject and not liking the one I brought up, mentioned peacekeeping. This is quite a different role than the ordinary role of peacekeeping.
An interesting article appeared in the London Times on November 30, 1978. It must have been one of the final editions of that newspaper. It dealt with an Independent Television News team which was back after spending 110 days in Angola. They went down there trying to locate Dr. Jonas Savimbi's Unita movement. As I understand from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, our troops will be positioned along the Namibia-South Angola border. What is happening just over that border surely will be of interest to the troops. Dr. Savimbi's Unita movement is in there fighting a guerrilla war against the Cuban and Russian-backed Angolan government forces.
This team was ambushed at the start of the offensive against Unita in which, the report says, the MPLA forces used French built Puma troop-carrying helicopters piloted by East Germans. The Angola ground troops were also being commanded by East Germans at platoon level, and between 30 and 50 Cuban tanks were also used in the operation. When you realize that SWAPO troops were also sequestered just over that border we can realize the situation that Canadian and other
December 12, 1978

UN forces will be in when they occupy that position, for whatever reason.
I am certain this is not a peacekeeping operation as outlined by Mitchell Sharp when he gave his famous eight criteria for peacekeeping operations. If I had a minute I should like to read them so that we may find out how they differ from the situation we find in Namibia. They are as follows:
There must be a threat to international peace and security that requires the establishment of a peacekeeping force.
The peacekeeping endeavour should be linked to an agreement for a political settlement, or at least a reasonable expectation of a negotiated settlement.
They are not even close to a political settlement there, and I expect it will be years before there is a political settlement.
To continue with the criteria:
The peacekeeping force should be responsible to a political authority, preferably the United Nations.
The sponsoring authority should receive reports and have adequate powers to supervise the mandate of the force.
The parties to the conflict must accept the peacekeeping force.
Canadian participation in force must be acceptable to all concerned.
We may be acceptable to SWAPO, we may be acceptable to South Africa, but i doubt very much that we are acceptable to all forces involved there.
The criteria continue as follows:
The peacekeeping force must have a clear mandate, including provision for freedom of movement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has disputed the peacekeeping nature of this particular force. Perhaps it might be of some benefit to report briefly some of the facts.
Canada has been an active member of the group of five western countries attempting to arrange a peaceful resolution of the Namibia problem. The basic feature of the proposal made by Canada, France, the Federal Republic of Germany, the United Kingdom and the U.S.A. for an internationally acceptable settlement in Namibia concerns the holding of fair and free elections in the territory, under the supervision and control of the United Nations.
Adjournment Debate
After acceptance by South Africa and the Southwest Africa People's Organization of the western proposal, the Secretary General of the United Nations prepared a plan which sets out how the United Nations would fulfil its responsibilities for supervision and control of the elections. The Security Council has approved this plan, and to give effect to its provisions has authorized the establishment of the United Nations Transition Assistance Group, UNTAG.
UNTAG will have a military component up to an authorized limit of 7,500 personnel, as well as a civilian unit of approximately 1,900 persons. It is the responsibility of the UN Secretary General to consult with all parties concerned on the composition of the UN force, on the date for its deployment to Namibia, and on the mandate that will govern its operation.
As one of the authors of the western proposal on Namibia, as an active participant in the negotiations that led up to its acceptance by South Africa and SWAPO, and as a nation that has traditionally played an active role in promoting peaceful settlement of international disputes, Canada has a strong interest in a successful resolution to the Namibia problem under the aegis of the United Nations.
One of our continuing objectives has been to help strengthen the capacity and the authority of the United Nations in its role as a peacekeeping agency. Canada has consistently responded to UN requests to provide personnel for peacekeeping duties. As a result of this lengthy and intensive experience Canada has become recognized for its excellence in this field, both for its objectivity and the professional competence of its troops. Our experience has also provided us with a good degree of insight into the successes and failures of present and past peacekeeping operations.
With respect to Namibia, when the conditions and terms of reference are established, should a request come from the UN Secretary General for a contribution to UNTAG, the government would give serious consideration to it to determine whether the operation holds promise of success and whether Canada can play a useful role in it.
